Lexifina · results report · generated 12 November 2026, 23:36

caselaw-lean-2

caselaw-lean-2 is the second Lean model of US precedent, run over every decision in our record of US case law. v1 checked one thing: whether a whole decision was validly overruled, by court rank. v2 models what courts do with precedent at the level of holdings: graded authority, same-case history, partial overruling, supersession by statute, and circuit splits. No treatment is believed unless Lean's checker admits it with a certificate: the court's own words, at a stated offset, in the majority opinion. The results are tested against courts' own later notes, the Supreme Court Database, the Constitution Annotated table and published lists of congressional overrides.

A Lean proof shows that a status follows from our encoding of doctrine and from the treatments Lean admitted. It does not show that the encoding matches what courts do. The held-out evaluation in section 10 measures that.

2. Why v1 was small, and what v2 adds

v1's model was small because its ambition was narrow. It held the structure of precedent: a court sits in a system and a tier, a court binds those below it, a court may overrule only its own or lower courts' decisions, and an overruling counts from the day it is decided. The courts and decisions were its input, not part of it. What a decision holds, which part was overruled, whether a statute had since rewritten the words a decision read: none of that was in Lean. It sat in a Python reader that Lean trusted.

The v1 post listed five ways to grow it: holdings rather than decisions, the finer rules of authority, abrogation by statute, the reader inside the proof, and substance where the law is rule-like. v2 does the first four. Rule-like substance is in v2 only as Horty's factor model of precedential constraint, which is proved and has now been run on real factors: 44 binding bases, 43 consistent (section 6).

3. Design research

Six research notes were written before and during the build. The first three shaped the draft design; the last three, on how large formalisms keep their statements honest, produced the revised design (DESIGN.md, D1–D9), which supersedes the draft where they differ.

Doctrine: the US law of precedent as a specification

A rule-by-rule account of US precedent written to be translated: the Supreme Court's vertical authority, horizontal stare decisis in each circuit and state intermediate court, federal courts on state law and the reverse, courts of last resort by jurisdiction, unpublished-opinion rules with their dates, the treatment vocabulary, timing, abrogation by statute, and holdings versus dicta. Each rule carries a tag: S checked, L leading case from memory, U uncertain.

What we took: The graded Force scale, dated court epochs with successions and adoptions, the parameter tables (horizontal, trialScope, unpubForce, …), the two event families (same-case history and later-case treatment), the two-date status query, and the §9 checklist that became the authority theorems. U rows became table parameters, never theorem premises (D2).

Prior art: theories of precedent, citators, datasets

A survey of formal theories of precedent (Horty's result and reason models, Prakken, Canavotto, Lamond, HYPO/CATO, ANGELIC), citation-network authority, commercial and open citators and their measured accuracy, datasets of overrulings, legal formalisms (Catala, L4, Blawx) and LLM extraction pitfalls.

What we took: Certificate-gated admission with a disqualifier list inside Lean; Horty consistency and forcing (Spec/Horty); binding sub-bases and the split definition; partial overruling as removing a holding; the derived atRisk finding; separate kinds for history, reported treatment and the court's own act; and the held-out gold sets (SCDB, the Constitution Annotated table, Christiansen–Eskridge).

Data audit: what the corpus can support, measured

A stratified sample of the corpus, read from git, measuring what each field and marker supports: front-matter coverage, how much opinion text exists, whether majority and dissent are separated, status markers in the header zone, how often each treatment phrase occurs, mis-tiered courts, district recovery for intermediate courts, the statute links, and compute.

What we took: Header-zone rules for bench, publication and form; the re-tiering of mis-tiered appeals courts; units from dockets, counties and judges; later courts' notes held out as gold; and streaming every file from git instead of checking out the corpus.

No external sources: every figure is measured on a sample of 55,285 decision files read from git.

caselaw-lean-2/research/data_audit.md, 441 lines

Formalizing CPython: registry, audit, differential tests

The CPython 3.15.2 Lean model (Andrews and Zhang): a function-by-function mirror of the C source, a registry of every property with a locked statement, refuted properties kept with counterexamples, differential runs against the real interpreter, and coverage reported against the full denominator.

What we took: Registry.lean plus a statement lock (D2); refute, never weaken; the mutation kill matrix as the mechanical form of "would a broken version pass?" (D3); an independent Python reference with four-way triage of every disagreement (D4); and attributing each finding to the mechanism that found it.

The revised design, D1–D9 (DESIGN.md)

Sources: AlphaProof Code (comparator, locked statements, trust inventory, spec-deviation log), the broyojo Python formalization (registry + Audit.lean, refute-don't-weaken, mutation "would a broken version pass?", differential runs vs the real system), AWS Cedar (small readable spec, DRT vs implementation, generic lemmas), seL4/CompCert (layered refinement, prose assumption list), Catala (default calculus: exceptions, conflicts as errors → for us, as findings), verified-checker pattern (untrusted solver + small checker), OpenFisca (no silent defaults).

D1. Three layers, one trust boundary

  1. Spec (CaseLaw2/Spec/*): short, readable, propositional definitions of precedent — force, canChangeStatus, goodLaw (two-date), split — written as Catala-style labelled default trees (each rule a default with named exceptions: Erie, Marks, adoption, unpublished, en banc, succession…), parameterised by an abstract Rules structure. Every rule carries the doctrine.md id it implements. Target: a lawyer can read it next to doctrine.md.
  2. Exec (CaseLaw2/Exec/*): decidable, efficient functions over Array/HashMap with proved equivalence (exec_force_eq_spec, exec_status_eq_spec, checkCert_sound, …). Generic lemmas proved once: status is a fold over events; same-day events on distinct holdings commute; partial events touch only their holdings; revival.
  3. Untrusted (Python + LLM readers, data tables): may be wrong; nothing it produces is believed unless an Exec checker admits it with a certificate. Ship certificates as files anyone can re-check.

D2. Statement lock (comparator-style)

  • CaseLaw2/Registry.lean: every public theorem by name with its statement; tools/caselaw2/audit/audit.py (or Lean #guard_msgs-based Audit.lean) checks each registered theorem's type is exactly the locked statement and its axioms ⊆ {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}. No sorry, axiom, native_decide in theorems. Statement changes go through a logged change request (STATEMENTS.log): weakening = escalate as probable data/spec bug; a false property is refuted (counterexample kept as a #guard), never silently weakened.
  • Doctrine as hypotheses/parameters, never axioms; U-tagged rows never premises (two Rules instances: firm S/L only, all incl. U; output rows carry firm=1 when both agree).

D3. Falsifiability (mutation + replay)

  • ~15 deliberately broken variants of force/status/checkCert (e.g. Erie both ways, panel overrules panel, ignore unpublished, ignore partial scope, statute supersession retroactive, revival ignored, cert accepts dissents) — each registered theorem/property must FAIL on ≥1 mutant (checked by #guard counterexamples on small instances); each rule must have ≥1 real decision that exercises it; known episodes replay (Betts/Gideon, Bowers/Lawrence, Kentucky 1976, Bonner, South Corp, Ledbetter, a California CoA conflict, a partial overruling).

D4. Differential testing

  • An independent Python reference implementation of force/status (written from doctrine.md by a different agent, not from the Lean) run on all real data + generated inputs; every disagreement triaged (Lean spec, Python ref, data).
  • External oracles scored separately: later courts' typed notes, SCDB precedentAlteration, CRS table, Congress override lists, SCOTUS split resolutions. Every disagreement with an oracle is OUR error until triaged into: reader wrong / checker too strict / oracle wrong / genuinely contested.

D5. No silent defaults

  • Unknown = Option/explicit unknown constructors in Lean (TSV 0 parses to none). Three-valued status outputs: negative-treatment-admitted / none-admitted / unknown(reason).

D6. Spec-deviation log + trust inventory

  • DEVIATIONS.md: every place the Lean rules differ from doctrine.md (simplifications, U rows, unmodelled states).
  • TRUST.md (seL4-style prose list): what is proved (kernel), proved-by-computation, certificate-checked (compiled checker, trusts the Lean compiler), tested (differential/oracle), assumed (doctrine tables, reader for holdings text), with trusted line counts (Spec + statement registry) vs untrusted.

D7. Coverage reported honestly

  • Pinned corpus manifest (all 6.9M nodes, repo commits); per layer: accepted / written / not started; per-court and per-decade coverage; which method produced each finding (rule, reader, oracle).

D8. Explanations

  • Every verdict row carries a justification tree id (rule path through the default tree + certificate ids), rendered s(CASP)-style in the report for samples.

D9. Build/run

  • Approved: separate Lake package caselaw-lean-2/runner/ requiring lean-proofs by path, compiled lean_exe (state in TRUST.md that checks run compiled). No Mathlib (Lean 4.35, no Finset): lists with decidable membership; Nat keys interned by the runner; string checks only in certificate checkers with structural soundness proofs.
  • Approved SCHEMA additions: optional factors.tsv (holding_id, factor, side, inReason) for Horty reasons; system rules for CA review-granted force; Tax Court appeal venue (Golsen) and Texas TRAP 41.3 transfer source as per-decision optional columns appeal_venue, transfer_from in an optional decisions2_extra.tsv.

4. Architecture: three layers, one trust boundary

Spec. Short, readable definitions of precedent, written as labelled default trees: each rule a default with named exceptions (Erie, Marks, adoption, unpublished, en banc, succession), each label tied to the doctrine rule it implements. Doctrine tables enter as parameters, so every theorem holds for any table.

Exec. The same functions over hash maps, fast enough for the corpus, with proved equality to the Spec.

Untrusted. Python and LLM readers and the doctrine tables. They may be wrong. A treatment or history row is admitted only if the compiled certificate checker passes it, and its soundness theorem says what passing means.

The statement lock

  • audit/audit.py check lists every theorem from the Lean environment (audit/ListTheorems.lean). It then elaborates #check @thm and #print axioms thm (lean --json) and compares each with audit/statements.lock. It also checks that the axioms are within {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}, and that no CaseLaw2 source contains sorry, admit, native_decide or an axiom declaration. Exit 1 on any problem.
  • audit/audit.py lock --reason "..." accepts the current statements. It rewrites statements.lock, Registry.lean and Audit.lean, and appends every new, changed or removed statement to STATEMENTS.log.
  • Policy:
    • a weakened statement is escalated as a probable spec or data bug;
    • a false property is refuted (its counterexample kept, as with revival_counterexample), never weakened.
  • Audit.lean is part of lake build LegalProofs.CaseLaw2, so a changed statement fails the build itself.

Mutation testing

Each registered property must fail on at least one deliberately broken model. 27 properties were run against 27 mutants; every property holds of the Spec, and every mutant is caught. The matrix is in section 5.

Differential testing

The Lean runner (runner/, the Spec through the Exec layer) was compared with an independent Python reference (lean-proofs/tools/caselaw2/ref/precedent_ref.py, written from doctrine.md). The comparison ran on:

  • the fixtures;
  • about 55,000 generated universes;
  • the real data that has landed so far.

Every disagreement was triaged into one of four classes:

  • (a) the Lean is wrong against doctrine.md;
  • (b) the reference is wrong;
  • (c) doctrine.md leaves the point open: one reading was chosen and recorded in both DEVIATIONS.md (items 30–54) and REF_NOTES.md ("Revisions after differential testing");
  • (d) a data or fixture error.

Both sides were then fixed until they agreed.

Headline, final (12 Nov, evening; §8). Run under Linux Lean 4.35.0 in WSL, after the fuzz fixes and the hunt fixes (H2, H3b, H4, H6):

  • Generated sweep: 1,000 fresh universes (seeds 53000–53999, with the new hunt layer) give zero disagreements over 344,828 compared keys.
  • Regression set: 111 kept counterexamples, all agreeing.
  • Real data (fresh snapshot with the corrected bench and publication labels; 6,892,454 decisions, 48,318,876 edges): certs 0 of 346,832, splits 0 of 329, conflicts 0 of 107; status 5 of 394,963 (0.0013%) and findings 6 of 133,588 (0.0045%), all eleven of them firm flags only, one open class (§8.4).
  • lake build LegalProofs.CaseLaw2 green; audit.py check: 114 theorems, 0 statement changes, 0 problems.

Headline, first pass (12 Nov, afternoon).

  • Final sweep: 5,000 fresh universes (seeds 20000–24999) give zero disagreements over 881,886 compared keys.
  • Stress sweep: 2,000 universes twice the size (seeds 30000–31999) give 2 firm-flag-only differences over 737,019 keys, explained in §4.
  • Regression set: 110 kept counterexamples, all agreeing.
  • Real data (snapshot of 12 Nov 18:00, with reader and interim holdings files): certs 0 of 218,200, status 17 of 78,615 (0.022%), findings 27 of 83,686 (0.032%). Splits are 0 of 0 because the holdings windows are malformed (d6). See "Real data".
  • Errors found: 71 classes. 26 were Lean errors, 17 were reference errors, 24 were open points settled with one reading (c), and 4 were data or contract problems (d). Comparison-layer artifacts are listed separately.
  • Statement lock: no theorem statement changed. lake build LegalProofs.CaseLaw2 is green, and audit/audit.py check reports 84 theorems, 0 statement changes and 0 problems. No sorry, axiom or native_decide.

Rounds, classes and fuzzing are in section 11.

  • M13 order-dependent status
  • M14 soft treatments count
  • M15 no power check
  • M16 resolver ignores precedence
  • M17 effects before their date
  • M18 cert off-by-one offsets
  • M19 cert trusts window text
  • M20 cert ignores citation index
  • M21 status global after adoption cut-off
  • M22 divisions overrule the court
  • M23 line rows report the union status
  • M24 splits and conflicts on the union status
  • M25 Horty base keeps precedents overruled in the line
  • M26 heir rows drop effects that reach every line

Real-case replays

145 #guard checks in Examples.lean run on every build. The episodes:

  • Betts/Gideon and Bowers/Lawrence (status by date, power, H1 self); a district court citing Bowers in 2005 (citesOverruled).
  • Kentucky 1976. A 1970 old Court of Appeals decision binds the new Court of Appeals in 1990, which cannot overrule it; the Supreme Court of Kentucky can (lastResortSelf).
  • Bonner. Pre-split 5th Cir. law binds the 11th; post-split law is persuasive; panel no, en banc yes.
  • South Corp. CCPA law binds the Federal Circuit, and district courts on patent law only.
  • M.A.P. v. Ryan. Cross-system adoption: pre-1971 D.C. Cir. law binds D.C. courts; later law does not.
  • Erie both ways and on both sides of 1938.
  • California Court of Appeal conflict. The superior court gets both answers (choice); under an own-unit rule it follows its district; a SCOTUS holding ends the conflict.
  • Georgia partial overruling. Notice falls, venue stands, the anonymous issue is unknown:partialScope.
  • Ledbetter. Superseded for conduct from 28 May 2007, known from 29 Jan 2009.
  • The 5th Cir. 1996 unpublished cut-off.
  • A Sunburst prospective overruling.
  • Revival.
  • En banc grant under an unknown rule -> unknown.
  • Status per line (round 2). The Salinas / Adamson decision has two status rows, orig overruled and the Eleventh Circuit's good; a conflict between it and a later Eleventh Circuit panel exists in the Eleventh Circuit and not in the Fifth; a Horty base holding both is inconsistent in the Eleventh's line and consistent in the Fifth's. A pre-1971 D.C. Circuit decision that court later overruled en banc is still good law for the D.C. Court of Appeals and the Superior Court (M.A.P.). The Federal Circuit en banc reaches every line of a CCPA decision (the original court is gone).
  • Certificates. Gideon's own words are admitted; a wrong offset, a dissent, a wrong target, no power, a procedural "point of error is overruled" and a reported "overruled by" are all rejected.

Trust tiers

What a reader must believe, in seL4's style. The trusted Spec is what a lawyer would read against doctrine.md; the glue is tested, not proved.

Where it ran: Windows Application Control blocks the Windows Lean toolchain and the compiled caselaw2.exe on this machine, so the build, the statement audit and every run reported here were made under Linux Lean 4.35.0 in WSL Ubuntu (elan's official toolchain, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu), with the runner compiled as a native Linux executable (run_lean_wsl.sh; LEAN.md "Running under WSL"). The sources are the Windows tree, copied unchanged. The trust in the Lean compiler (below) is therefore trust in the Linux toolchain's compiler.

Proved (kernel)

These are lake build LegalProofs.CaseLaw2, audit/audit.py check and LegalProofs/CaseLaw2/Audit.lean.

  • 141 theorems, all listed in Registry.lean and in LEAN.md (4 for witness rows in round 4, 6 added in the five-limits pass, 1 for fuzz bug FB-L2, 9 for the hunt fixes, 14 in Hunt.lean, 23 in Spec/Lines.lean for round 2; each logged in STATEMENTS.log; no earlier statement changed). Last checked 12 Nov 23:25 under WSL: audit.py check reports 141 theorems, 4 with no axioms, 0 statement changes, 0 problems.
  • Each statement and axiom list is locked by #guard_msgs in Audit.lean, which is part of the build. A changed statement stops the build. audit.py lock --reason is the only way to accept a change, and it logs the change in STATEMENTS.log.
  • Spec theorems:
    • authority §9 22(a)–(d);
    • power (no panel overrules a panel under a strong rule; no lower court over a higher; only SCOTUS over SCOTUS; no cross-system power; no power over later decisions);
    • status (order independence, partial scope, prospectivity, supersession, monotonicity with the revival counterexample, soft and inferred treatments inert);
    • resolver and splits (soundness, SCOTUS resolves);
    • Horty (consistency closed under removal, forcing, result ⊑ reason, answer embedding);
    • findings sanity;
    • certificate soundness, window hashes (checkCert_window_hash) and citation-index resolution (checkCert_cite_index);
    • the new atRisk families (claimRisk_needs_no_power, soft_claim_disjoint, contraryBinding_needs_binding).
  • Refinement theorems: exec_lookups_eq_spec, exec_eventLookups_eq_spec, exec_force_eq_spec, exec_canChangeStatus_eq_spec and exec_status_eq_spec. All rest on one generic lemma, index_getD.
Proved by computation (`#guard`, evaluated by the compiler at build time)
  • 211 #guards:
    • 133 real-case replays in Examples.lean (35 of them for round 2);
    • 44 in Hunt.lean;
    • 16 SHA-1 vectors;
    • 14 Horty examples;
    • 3 mutation-matrix guards in Mutants.lean;
    • 1 registry count.
  • Mutation (D3): 26 properties against 26 mutants. Every property holds of the Spec, every property is killed by at least one mutant, and every mutant is caught. The matrix is in LEAN.md.
  • #guard trusts the compiler, unlike decide. The concrete theorem revival_counterexample uses kernel decide.
Certificate-checked (compiled checker; trusts the Lean compiler)
  • Treatment and history rows: admitted only when Cert.check returns ok or okUnverifiedBy. checkCert_sound proves admission implies every condition:
    • known text hash;
    • covering window;
    • the quote at the stated character offset;
    • a cue of the asserted kind;
    • no disqualifier;
    • target evidence present, and, when cite_index.tsv is supplied, a cite: evidence resolves through the index to the row's target node (checkCert_cite_index: index(compact cite) = target);
    • majority, plurality or per curiam part;
    • date order;
    • power (ok) or an unknown deciding court (okUnverifiedBy).
  • Holdings' sentences: checked for hash and quote at offset.
  • What this does not certify: that the reading is legally right. It only certifies that these words, at this place, in this part of this court's opinion, warrant the row (prior_art §5.6).
  • Window hashes are checked inside Lean (five-limits pass). When window_sha.tsv is supplied, every window the checker uses (for the quote and for the target context) must have a recorded digest, and the checker computes the SHA-1 of the window text itself (Sha1.hex, pure Lean, no FFI; 16 #guard test vectors from Python hashlib) and compares. checkCert_window_hash proves: an admitted row's quote sits in a well-formed window whose computed SHA-1 equals the recorded digest. Each digest is computed once per run and cached in a Thunk that Window.digest_eq pins to Sha1.hex text.
  • What stays outside Lean: window_sha.tsv is written by tools/caselaw2/window_sha.py, which reads each decision from git HEAD, checks that the file's SHA-1 equals text_sha, and hashes the normalised cut [start0, end0). So Lean checks window text = audit copy's window; that the audit copy's window is the corpus text at text_sha rests on that script (on snap5 all 336,242 windows matched their corpus cut).
Tested only
  • Glue: the runner's TSV translation and output, Run.lean, Data.lean and Tsv.lean (about 860 lines). It is exercised by fixtures/ (all 13 SCHEMA files, every output kind) and a full-scale load and citation pass on synthetic decisions (6.89M nodes, 6.04M citations).
  • Glue fuzzing (FUZZ.md, tools/caselaw2/fuzz/):
    • Run A, 300 cases with Lean: the loaders reject and log every row SCHEMA rejects and parse every other row to the oracle's values; a re-serialised row loads back identically; Cert.quoteOk and its slice match Python's code-point slicing.
    • Run B: 5,000 cases against the reference only. Its Lean half awaits Application Control.
    • Every real certificate (346,835 rows) was recomputed in Python; there are 0 disagreements with the runner.
    • The open Lean bugs FB-L1 to FB-L8 are in FUZZ_BUGS.md.
  • The Horty check in the runner (factors.tsv) has not been exercised on fixtures.
  • Differential testing (D4) against the independent Python reference: done, see DIFFTEST.md. The final sweep of 5,000 fresh generated universes leaves a residual of under 0.01% of compared keys, all triaged. The real data run so far (supersessions on all 6.9M decisions) shows no disagreement.
  • The split rows are decided in the runner glue (DESIGN layer 5 pairwise test) and are tested only. The Spec's split/scotus_resolves_split back the conflict rows.
Assumed
  • The doctrine tables: courts2, succession, adoption and system_rules, with their S/L/U tags.
    • Theorems never assume a row.
    • Verdicts carry firm = 1 when the S/L-only tables agree with the tables including U rows.
  • The readers: holdings text, issue keys, answers and Marks rows (held back by certificates for treatments and history; holdings only partly).

6. Data layers

Each layer was built by its own agent, to the contract in SCHEMA.md. None of them reads later courts' notes: those are the evaluation's gold.

Courts and decisions

What it is. Courts as dated epochs (tier, system, circuit, unit), successions and adoptions between courts, per-system and per-court rules of precedent, and one row per decision with its court, unit, bench, publication, form and the SHA of its text. Labels come from rules over each decision's header region, read once from git.

Gaps (COURTS.md)
  • bench
    • It is unknown for 3.19M decisions, mostly state courts of last resort, because there is no header cue. They are not assumed to be whole-court.
    • About 1 in 5 enBanc labels is still an order on a rehearing petition rather than a decision of the en banc court.
    • The en banc / circulated re-read (labels_fix2.py) covers only the 15,690 decisions that overrule, disapprove or recede. Even there about one in four en banc decisions is still panel: three-judge courts where the panel was the whole court, Alabama's appellate courts (always a full court), Louisiana five-judge benches, and decisions with no judges line. A court-size rule would be needed.
    • conflictPanel has only 5 samples (60%).
  • Units
    • Not recovered for about 38% of the decisions of unit-structured intermediate courts. The weakest are TX (45%), CA (55%), IN (56%) and NY AD (61%), mostly pre-1980 decisions with bare numeric dockets and no judge match.
    • NY Appellate Term, the OK Court of Civil Appeals and Tennessee are almost unrecovered.
    • Re-fetching CAP head_matter (which carries the court line) would close most of this gap; that was not attempted here.
    • County tables are the current ones:
      • Ohio: districts 11 and 12 are applied only from 1976.
      • Louisiana: applied from 1960.
      • Florida and Texas: no county tables are used, because their county-to-district maps changed or overlap.
  • Recall is not measured. The precision figures say nothing about recall. Header-only en banc and plurality detection misses en banc or plurality decisions whose header says nothing. Plurality is especially conservative: 199 decisions.
  • Publication
    • published relies on CAP's near-constant precedential_status. A reported state decision that a later court depublished is still "published": depublication is a same-case event and belongs in history.tsv.
    • Reporter check (labels_fix2.py): 8,022 reporter-cited decisions stay non-published because they say so themselves or are entries under 600 characters. A Florida per curiam of under 300 characters that cites an authority is still table.
    • The hunt's figure of 77,575 mislabelled decisions was too high: 50,512 are Florida PCAs without opinion and about 11,600 are T.C. Memo. / Summary Opinions, both correctly non-published. 7,342 were wrong and are fixed.
  • Form
    • SCOTUS memorandum orders (272,740) and short orders elsewhere (643,590) are form = memorandum. 371,105 stubs stay unknown: 48,586 at SCOTUS and 322,519 elsewhere (162,692 of those have no opinion text; the rest have no order language).
  • Doctrine tables
    • Rows marked U in doctrine.md stay U. The best readings are tagged U and are data, not premises.
    • Still uncertain: the California 1966 effective day; the Oklahoma 1959-03-11 date rests on a statutory history note (L); the end of the Delaware Court of Errors and Appeals in 1897 (day); TRAP 41.3's start (believed 2008-09-01, not confirmed; no row depends on it); the Ohio 2002 rule (secondary sources); the CNMI 2004 end of Ninth Circuit review (1 or 2 May).
  • Military courts stay tier S; CAAF binds the service Courts of Criminal Appeals through adoption.tsv.
  • Tribal courts are one system per tribe (1000–1022); their tiers are v1's (S), except Navajo (L), so a tribal appellate court does not yet bind its trial courts.
  • Unmapped: none. The 8 former 3160 decisions: 6 Department of the Interior land-office decisions → 10109 (federal, S); 1 Salina land-office register → 10110 (federal, S); Ex parte Rhodes (1816, "Judge's Chambers") → 10111, system 999 (state not identified; U).
  • Web checks (2026-11-12, limit 8): 19 of 25 searches; results above and in courts_validation.md §5. Earlier, 3 of the allowed 10 searches were used. They verified:
    • the Maryland 2022-12-14 renames;
    • Alabama Act No. 987, effective 1969-10-01;
    • D.C. Pub. L. 87-873, approved 1962-10-23 (effective date computed).
  • 2026-11-12 coordinator: added system_rules rows for CA reviewGrantedForce (system 5) and D.C. Court of Appeals court-level horizontal strong (court 627), the two data gaps DIFFTEST found.

Treatment reader

What it is. Regex candidates over full text, read by an LLM (gpt-5.4-mini; hard cases gpt-6.1-sol), which returns typed treatments and same-case history, each with the quoted words, their character offsets and the opinion part. The quote must be found in the text before a row is written. The reader never reads later courts' notes.

READER.md

Treatment and same-case history reader (caselaw-lean-2)

Outputs: treatments.tsv, history.tsv and cert_text.tsv, as specified in ../SCHEMA.md. Also written: reader_stats.json, reader_rejects.tsv, treatments_items.tsv (row → candidate id → how the quote was chosen), and reader_usage.json (tokens and cost per stage). The code is in global-law-lean/lean-proofs/tools/caselaw2/reader/, and the working files are in reader_work/, which holds no full texts.

Held-out rule
  • Inputs used: decision texts read from git (git cat-file --batch), graph/{nodes,cite_index,courts,edges.bin}.tsv and lean-in-v3/courts_named.tsv (tiers, joined by court name).
  • Never read: events_v3/reports.tsv and lean-in-v3/reports.tsv.
  • Later courts' notes are recognised only to reject them. Examples are "X, overruled [on other grounds] by Y", "(abrogated by Y)", "superseded by statute as stated in Y", "(overruling X)", "X was overruled in Y", and citator-style ", superseded by statute, ch. 63" straight after a citation (rules.REPORT, rules.CITATOR_BEFORE). None of them is ever kept as evidence.
  • Treatments are asserted only from the treating decision's own act-shaped words: we/this court + present verb, the present passive "is/are (hereby) Xed", "to the extent/insofar as … Xed", and "superseded by statute/rule/amendment" stated by the court itself.
  • History comes only from the reviewing decision's own present-tense disposition. Citation-string history of other cases is rejected.
Pipeline
  1. scan.py: candidate pass. It covers 152 repos and 6,931,555 files (39,101 parallel-reporter copies have no node), with 0 UTF-8 decode failures.
    • It looks for literal anchors, then runs the family regexes locally: overrule, disapprove, recede from, abrogate, supersede, limited to its facts, question/doubt/continued validity, decline to follow, and repudiate/abandon/no longer follow.
    • It splits each file into parts from its ## headings (Majority, Per Curiam, Lead/Plurality, Concurrence, Dissent, Head matter, Combined). Inside Majority/Combined sections, a short judge line ending "dissenting"/"concurring" starts a separate opinion (part suffix ~, exported as the base part).
    • Output: 2,576,683 treatment candidates and 2,351,591 disposition sentences. History candidates were kept only when the decision cites a case bearing its own party names.
  2. resolve.py: cheap filters and targets. Filtering left 65,822 candidates for the model. Rejections:
reasoncount
procedural ("objection/point of error … overruled")1,205,556
not act-shaped757,372
report240,926
separate opinion155,099
narrated past act98,922
no resolvable target43,636
head matter9,223
  • Target candidates come from citations in the ±400 window (via cite_index), plus names of the decisions the treating decision cites (as v1 did). For soft kinds (limited, questioned, declinedToFollow), the target must be named in the sentence itself.
  • History targets are cited decisions that satisfy all of the following:
    • they share two party tokens with the reviewing decision (or one, if a name has only one);
    • they are dated within 8 years before it;
    • they come from a lower court of the same system (or the same court, for withdrawn, reinstated and rehearing en banc granted); SCOTUS may review state courts;
    • they match the body the sentence names (court of appeals, trial court, or an agency, which is rejected).
  1. classify.py: model reading.
    • gpt-5.4-mini (Azure US East 2): 65,576 items, 5 per call, JSON schema.
    • The model returns own_act, kind, targets (ids from the resolved list only; 82 invented ids were dropped), scope, issue labels, temporal and an exact quote.
    • Hard subset re-read by gpt-6.1-sol (hard.py): status-changing kinds where the model chose among two or more candidates, had confidence below 0.95, scoped the act to issues, or the sentence names another court acting. That is 16,395 items; its answers override the small model's.
    • gpt-6-sol was never used.
  2. certify.py: certificates. For each row it checks:
    • the quote is found exactly in the window (only whitespace runs and quote-mark styles are tolerated, and the window's own text is used);
    • text[start:end] equals the quote (asserted);
    • the quote contains a cue of the kind (rules.CUES); otherwise the focus sentence is used if that sentence has the cue;
    • the quote is not inside another court's quotation (curly-quote check; a quote starting “ or [T]);
    • the target evidence (cite: normalised citation, or name: token) occurs in text[start-400:end+400].

Offsets are characters of the git-HEAD text, UTF-8 decoded with CRLF→LF. The quote and window are normalised tab/newline→space (one for one). Duplicate (by, target, kind, scope) rows keep the most confident one.

Authority (court power) is not filtered. 519 rows have a lower court treating a SCOTUS decision, and 154 rows have SCOTUS as the treating court. Lean decides.

Cue table (what certify.py requires in a quote)
kindcues
overruledoverrul, repudiat, abandon, no longer follow, no longer good law, no longer the law, no longer be followed, no longer adhere
disapproveddisapprov
recededFromreced
abrogatedabrogat
supersededByEnactmentsupersed, legislatively overruled, abrogat
limitedlimit
questionedquestion, doubt, no longer good law, no longer valid, continued/continuing validity/vitality
criticizedcriticiz, criticis
declinedToFollowdecline, refuse, not follow, no longer follow, no longer be followed, not be followed, not adhere, unwilling, not inclined
distinguisheddistinguish
followedfollow

History cues are affirm, revers, vacat/set aside/quash/annul, modif, denied, granted, dismiss, en banc, withdr, reinstat, refused and publish.

Field mapping
  • scope: all, issues:<slugs>, partialUnknown ("to the extent inconsistent…") or otherGrounds.
  • temporal: unknown unless the opinion says otherwise. "Prospective" with no date becomes prospectiveFrom:<treating decision date>.
  • explicit: always 1.
  • reader: gpt-5.4-mini or gpt-6.1-sol.
  • confidence: the model's own figure.
  • history src: hist-regex-v2:<mode>:<verb>. The mode records where the target evidence sits:
modemeaning

Precision (frozen held-out audit, blind)

Rules were frozen before the main run. Development samples dev1, dev2, dev3 and devh were used to fix rules, and their ids were excluded from this audit.

  • Sample: 160 admitted treatments (stratified by kind), 40 rejected candidates (20 rejected by the model or the certificate check, 20 by the cheap filters) and 40 history rows (stratified by kind).
  • Reviewers: five subagents read them shuffled, without the reader's kind or scope. They read the full git text when the window was not enough.
  • Files: reader_work/audit/heldout/ (packs, blind_*.jsonl, verdicts_*.jsonl, score.json).

Known gaps
  • Recall is unmeasured. Only 40 rejected candidates were reviewed (1 miss). Not-act-shaped sentences (757k) are rejected by rule, without reading.
  • distinguished, followed and criticized are not extracted at corpus scale. They appear only incidentally.
  • Content-filtered items: a few batches were refused by Azure's content filter. Those items (and 14 with no answer) are not yet retried one at a time.
  • Issue scope labels are the model's short free-text slugs, not issues.tsv keys. Agreement on scope is only 53%.
  • History has three blind spots. First, decisions that review an unpublished or non-corpus lower judgment yield nothing. Second, SCOTUS memorandum orders with no "reported below" citation yield nothing. Third, head-matter or front-matter history notes are not used. 36,254 history rows were dropped because the target was cited too far from the disposition and no shared party name appears in the window.
  • Temporal is read only from the window plus up to two prospectivity sentences of the same opinion.
  • Parts: inferred parts (inside Combined or Majority sections) are exported as plain majority/dissent/concurrence. The ~ marker is kept only in reader_work.
  • 2026-11-12 coordinator: treatments.tsv scope for partialUnknown/issues rows replaced by holdings_reach.tsv canonical issue keys (issues:<issue_key>) or 'all' where the reach step mapped the act; original kept as treatments.pre_reach.tsv.
  • 2026-11-12 data fix (limit 9): 2,287 of the 2,288 writRefused rows were Louisiana Supreme Court 'Writ refused.' (refusal to review), relabelled kind other; 1 Texas row kept. See COURTS.md.

Read so far: every Supreme Court item and 960 items of courts of last resort.

Holdings, issues and splits

What it is. Holdings for Supreme Court decisions and for every decision that is a treatment target or source, each with its issue, a yes/no answer where the issue is a split question, and the certified sentence that states it. Statutory issues are keyed by US Code subsection so splits can be found.

HOLDINGS.md

Holdings, issues, Marks rows and circuit-split data (agent: holdings)

Written 2026-11-12. Scripts: ~\Documents\global-law-lean\lean-proofs\tools\caselaw2\holdings\. Working files: data/holdings_work/ (raw model outputs, split windows, clusters, validation sets, verdicts).

Files (SCHEMA)
filerowsnotes
issues.tsv255,981244k decision-local issues d<node>.i<k>; 11,996 split questions usc:<title>:<section>(<sub>):q<n> with a canonical yes/no question; Marks-only issues d<node>.m<k>
holdings.tsv260,054243,258 decision holdings (ids H<node>.<k>), 16,796 split holdings (ids S<node>.<usc>.<k>, answer yes/no)
marks.tsv751326 fragmented SCOTUS decisions; tag U (model reading, never a premise)
holdings_cert_text.tsvone row per certificate windowtext_sha, start0 = max(0, start−400), end0 = min(len, end+400), window = normalised text[start0:end0]
holdings_reach.tsvextra (not in SCHEMA)by_node, target_node, scope (all, issues:k1,k2 or partialUnknown), src, confidence: which target holdings a v1 overruling act reaches, for acts whose words limit their scope
  • Quotes and certificates.
    • Every quote is a sentence span cut by our splitter from the court's own opinion part. The model only picks a sentence number, so it never types a quote.
    • assemble.py re-reads every decision from git HEAD. It checks sha1(bytes) = text_sha, and that the quote equals normalised text[start:end] (\r\n→\n, tab/newline→space).
    • check_certs.py repeats the check independently, including each window against text[start0:end0]: 0 failures (see holdings_work/check_certs.json).
  • Roles.
    • part = role. It is majority by default and perCuriam from the opinion heading or the courts agent's form.
    • It is plurality when decisions2.tsv or the syllabus line ("announced the judgment …") says plurality. Exception: the Marks reader lists that issue as joined by a majority (630 relabelled).
    • For Combined (CourtListener) texts, the opinion is cut at the first "…, dissenting/concurring" line.
  • target_evidence. It is cite:<title> U.S.C. § <sub> when the quote names the section, else name:-. A holding has no target decision.
  • Domain. It comes from the model's law field and the court's system: federalGeneral, federalPatent (title 35), federalTax (title 26), stateLaw:<system>. It is unknown for state law read in federal courts (Erie).
What was read (coverage)
streamdecisionsreadgaps
SCOTUS full opinions (opinion text ≥ 1,000 chars)30,28628,9521,265 had under 600 chars of opinion text after removing head matter; 69 were blocked by the Azure content filter
Treatment decisions: both sides of every v1 act (events_v3/acts.tsv), minus 2,266 acts where a lower court "overrules" SCOTUS44,229 (+368 that are SCOTUS full opinions)43,537485 had no opinion text; 145 were blocked by the content filter; 62 were unfinished when the final was written (gpt-6-luna stragglers)
Split citations: (subsection, court of appeals or SCOTUS decision)12,82312,8234 of 297 subsections could not be clustered (content filter)
  • Models.
    • gpt-5.4-mini read 187,893 decision holdings and all split extractions.
    • gpt-6-luna read 55,365 decision holdings: half of the SCOTUS and treat queues after 17:38. The reader column says which model read each row.
    • gpt-6.1-sol did the clustering, the second reading of split holdings, and Marks.
  • Holdings yield. 78,617 decisions have ≥ 1 holding; the mean is 3.3 per decision.
  • Treatments.
    • The reader's treatments.tsv did not exist when this ran, so the treatment set is v1 acts only. Rerunning extract_holdings.py on new targets plus reach.py --treatments extends it.
    • Decisions in acts whose words limit scope ("to the extent", "in part", "on other grounds", …) were read first.
  • Marks.
    • 555 SCOTUS decisions were flagged as fragmented: decisions2 plurality, or a syllabus "announced the judgment" / "delivered an opinion in which" line.
    • 326 have Marks rows. The rest had a majority on every issue, or no narrowest ground was found.
    • Rows with no logical-subset narrowest ground start "[no common denominator: result only]".
Method
  1. Holdings (extract_holdings.py).
    • Sentences of the court's own opinion are split with offsets.
    • A cue score (we hold/conclude/think, accordingly, plain meaning, …; citation strings dropped) picks 14 candidates, or 16 for SCOTUS, plus up to 3 "question presented" context sentences.
    • The model returns holdings by sentence id with issue label, proposition (≤ 300 chars), kind (holding, alternative or application), law, usc and confidence.
    • Dropped: confidence < 0.5, bare dispositions, non-candidate ids.
  2. Splits (splits_select.py → splits_windows.py → splits_extract.py → splits_cluster.py → split_verify.py).
    • The 300 subsections are the most-cited by courts-of-appeals decisions since 1995 in rows_out.tsv (18:3553(a) … 234 decisions at rank 300).
    • For each of 441,943 (subsection, decision) pairs: mentions in the court's part, a ±4-sentence window, and an interpretive-cue score (meaning, construe, plain language, lenity, sister circuits, split, …). Unpublished decisions are penalised.
    • Up to 40 courts-of-appeals decisions per subsection are taken round-robin across circuits, plus 12 SCOTUS decisions.
    • gpt-5.4-mini says whether the court interprets the subsection, and gives yes/no questions with answers. 80% of the chosen decisions were judged interpretive.
    • gpt-6.1-sol clusters each subsection's questions into canonical questions with polarity, so circuits line up on one issue_key.
    • gpt-6.1-sol then reads every split holding on an issue that ≥ 2 courts answered, in its ±400-char window. It rejected 2,955 of 8,214 (not this court's holding on that question) and corrected 103 answers.
  3. Split candidates (splits_report.py → holdings_work/split_candidates.tsv).
    • A candidate is two different circuits whose latest published holdings on the issue_key give opposite answers at some date, with confidence ≥ 0.6.
    • Lean's own test (neither binds the other, both good law on the date) is decided by the runner. This is the data-side count.
  4. Reach (reach.py). For 13,638 acts with limiting words, gpt-5.4-mini maps the act's window onto the target's numbered holdings.
    • holdings_reach.tsv has 13,629 rows: 8,546 name specific issue keys (12,959 keys, all present in issues.tsv), 400 reach the whole decision, and 4,683 are limited but match no listed holding (partialUnknown).
    • These rows are not audited.
Results
  • Split candidates: 190, over 11,996 canonical questions on 293 subsections.
  • Resolved later by SCOTUS: 27. SCOTUS answered the same issue_key after the split began.
  • Three examples:
    1. 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a): does "prison conditions" cover particular incidents such as excessive force?
      • Yes: Booth v. Churner, 206 F.3d 289 (3d Cir. 2000).
      • No: Nussle v. Willette, 224 F.3d 95 (2d Cir. 2000).
      • Resolved yes by Porter v. Nussle, 534 U.S. 516 (2002), which our SCOTUS row answers yes on the same issue_key.
    2. 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(5): does the first-to-file bar cease once the earlier action is no longer pending?
      • Yes: U.S. ex rel. Chovanec v. Apria Healthcare, 606 F.3d 361 (7th Cir. 2010).
      • No: United States v. Cellco P'ship, 748 F.3d 338 (D.C. Cir. 2014).
      • Resolved yes by Kellogg Brown & Root Servs. v. U.S. ex rel. Carter, 575 U.S. 650 (2015).
    3. 28 U.S.C. § 2255(e): does the saving clause allow § 2241 challenges to sentences, not only convictions?
      • Yes: Webster v. Daniels, 784 F.3d 1123 (7th Cir. 2015 en banc), and the 4th and 9th Circuits.
      • No: Reminsky v. United States, 523 F. App'x 327 (6th Cir. 2013; unpublished, so the published-only Lean test may not count that side).
      • Jones v. Hendrix (2023) is not in the selected SCOTUS set, so it shows as unresolved here.
Validation (blind; judges saw only the text window and the claim, not the model, confidence or group)

Judges were Claude subagents reading holdings_work/val/*.md. Verdicts are in val/judged_*.jsonl and scores in val/scores.json. Intervals are Wilson 95%.

measureresult95% CI

Split pairs before second reading: genuine split (same question, opposite, both holdings)11/30 = 0.370.22–0.55
Split pairs after second reading (final data): same question27/30 = 0.900.74–0.97
… same question and opposite answers25/30 = 0.830.66–0.93

  • Split holdings and the second reading. Of the 12 split holdings judged before the second reading:
    • the verifier rejected 4, and all 4 had failed;
    • the 8 it kept passed in 4 of 8.
    • So split holdings that are not on a split pair are still noisy. Use them for split detection only together with confidence.
  • Two "genuine" pairs share a circuit. In the verified 30, 2 genuine pairs were within one circuit, from the validation sampler's choice of example. splits_report.py now picks different circuits.
  • Known-split cases in the verified 30: Booth/Nussle; the 3d vs 11th Cir. FTCA proviso for TSOs; 2255(e); first-to-file; 1252(d) issue exhaustion; 924(c) multiple convictions; 3553(f) MDLEA.
  • Recall of the split detector against SCOTUS-resolved splits.
    • Gold: SCOTUS decisions in the 300 subsections that say they resolve a conflict among the courts of appeals. There are 302 conflict questions, each clustered onto an issue_key.
    • Where ≥ 2 circuits in our data had ruled on that issue_key before the SCOTUS decision, the detector found opposite answers in 20/51 = 0.39 (0.27–0.53).
    • Over all 302 it is 20/302 = 0.07 (0.04–0.10). Most misses are coverage: only 40 decisions per subsection were read, rows_out starts in 1995, and the split may have been on a narrower question.
  • Not validated: gpt-6-luna holdings (55,365 rows) were not in the blind sample, which was drawn before luna started, and Marks rows and reach rows were not audited. Treat luna rows' precision as unmeasured.
Tokens and cost
  • Tokens: 163.5M in total, over the 150M budget by 9%. The coordinator asked for maximum speed, which added the gpt-6-luna stream.
    • gpt-5.4-mini: 101.1M.
    • gpt-6-luna: 52.5M (reasoning tokens make it about 2× mini per call).
    • gpt-6.1-sol: 9.8M.
  • Cost about $346 at assumed list prices (see holdings_usage.json for the prices used). gpt-6-luna is priced as mini there, because its price was unknown.
  • Usage is logged per call to holdings_usage.jsonl. About 35 lines were lost to interleaved writes from parallel processes, an undercount of under 0.1%.
Gaps
  • 62 treatment decisions are unfinished, and 214 decisions plus 4 split subsections are blocked by the Azure content filter (mostly sexual-offence and violent-crime texts).
  • The reader's treatments.tsv is not yet joined (v1 acts only). Holdings of new targets need one more extract_holdings.py pass.
  • Plurality vs majority is per decision, refined only by the Marks reader's majority_issues. "Opinion of the Court with respect to Parts …" decisions are majority unless the Marks reader said otherwise.
  • Split coverage is bounded: 300 subsections and ≤ 40 circuit decisions each, chosen by cue score, from 1995 on.
  • Issue labels of decision-local holdings are not clustered across decisions. Only split questions share issue_keys across courts.
  • Validation used n = 60 and n = 30, so intervals are wide.

Statutes: law changes and supersession

What it is. Every rewrite of a US Code block that a decision cited, with the law, its enactment and effective dates and any retroactive reach; and candidate supersessions of a decision by a law, scored by the evidence that Congress had the decision in mind.

Counts.

  • lawchanges.tsv: 34,696 (law, US Code block) rewrites, each after at least one decision citing the block (1,931,153 citations, 1995 on). Dates from: llm 542, record 22,984, rx 11,170. Rows with retroactive_to set: 758.
  • supersessions.tsv: 13,977 rows over 6,385 decisions; by evidence: lawNamesDecision 256, quotedWordsStruck 12,265, reportNamesDecision 1,456; explicit = 1: 238; issue_key attached: 0; laterCourtSays rows: 0.
  • retroactive_to: 0 none; a yyyymmdd day = the earliest conduct/claim day the change reaches (before enactment); 1 = applies to matters pending on its effective date whatever the conduct date, no earlier bound stated. effective is the law's own effective date where it states one (src llm: or rx:), else the record's in-force day (src record:<how the record dated it>; record:enacted = dated on enactment because the record does not read effective dates).

Recall against Christiansen & Eskridge and Hasen:

  • Any evidence linking the decision to the overriding law: 23/36 (64%) (overrides work: 20/36). Explicit (law, report or court states it): 16/36 (44%). Score >= 0.5: 15/36 (42%).
  • Per item: statutes/recall2.tsv.

Strata: first10y = first rewrite of the cited block within 10 years (overrides census/samples); later = another rewrite or 10-15 years (new, blind reads here); cite = reporter cite in the law/report resolved to the decision, linked by section (new, blind reads here); SA/FT = Supreme Court + appeals / other courts. Audited pairs carry their verdict (0.97 / 0.03) as score; others the smoothed stratum precision (k+1)/(n+2).

Cost. The retroactivity reader used 1,170,337 tokens (gpt-5.4-mini). Everything else is regex and record reading.

Retroactivity extraction, accuracy
  • Calls: 242 (law x amended section, for the 34 confirmed overrides and the top 300 candidates), errors 0, tokens 1,170,337. Classes: appliesToPendingCases 11, asIfIncluded 4, noProvision 140, prospectiveOnly 66, retroactiveToDate 21.
  • Hand reads: subagents read the law text blind (no model output) and classified each item; RETRO_INSTRUCTIONS.md.
  • Final prompt/packet (v2) on a fresh hand-read sample [headline] (30): class 18/30 (60%); retroactive yes/no 25/30 (83%); effective date 21/30 (70%); retroactive_to 25/30 (83%).
  • First run (v1) on the first hand-read sample (blind) (30): class 17/30 (57%); retroactive yes/no 26/30 (87%); effective date 21/30 (70%); retroactive_to 26/30 (87%).
  • v2 on the first sample (used to diagnose v1, so optimistic) (30): class 19/30 (63%); retroactive yes/no 25/30 (83%); effective date 21/30 (70%); retroactive_to 25/30 (83%).
  • v1 -> v2: v1 packets missed the amending section when a tax law names "section N of the Internal Revenue Code" (no U.S.C. cite) and dropped passages that name the section by number; v1 also called a delayed effective date "noProvision".
Gaps (STATUTES.md)
  • Citations are read only from 1995 on, so block-level links start in 1995; earlier decisions enter only through a reporter cite in a law or report (cite stratum, linked by section).
  • Block rewrites the record credits to an edition rather than a law (174,795 first rewrites in the overrides work) have no law, so no row here.
  • Law texts: govinfo PLAW starts with the 104th Congress; earlier laws (Civil Rights Act of 1991, etc.) have no text (record:...:notext), so no effective-date reading and no naming evidence.
  • Effective dates for rows the LLM did not read come from regex rules over the law's effective-date passages (src rx:<kind>:sec<n>:rank<r>; rank 0 = in the amending section, 1 = names it, 2 = its title, 3 = Act-wide), or the record's in-force day. See the regex accuracy line above.
  • quotedWordsStruck covers only the first rewrite of a cited block (decision-text features were not recomputed for later rewrites).
  • Committee reports: only those listed in the law's legislative-history note, part 1 of multi-part reports.
  • explicit for unaudited rows: the naming passage contains override language (overrul, supersed, in response to, reject the, restore, clarify that, ...); the audits show naming alone often means codification (see the codifies counts).
  • laterCourtSays and issue_key depend on the reader's treatments.tsv and the holdings agent's holdings.tsv/issues.tsv; rows are added by rerunning s7_write.py and s9_validate.py when those files exist.

Source: caselaw-lean-2/data/STATUTES.md · caselaw-lean-2/data/lawchanges.tsv · caselaw-lean-2/data/supersessions.tsv

Horty factors

What it is. For Supreme Court holdings in 56 narrow question families (sub-families), the facts the Court found present and the ones it gave as its reason, each with a verbatim quote. They feed Horty's consistency check: a binding base must not order the same two reasons both ways.

Counts.

filerowsnotes
factors.tsv345v2. SCHEMA D9: holding_id, factor, side (pi or delta), inReason (0/1); 269 holdings, all H… rows of holdings.tsv. Replaced atomically (tmp + rename).
factor_vocab.tsv654v2: factor id, sub-family, family, side, name, definition, src. Ids are sub-family index×100 + k (56 sub-families).
factor_cases.tsv354Extra, not SCHEMA: holding_id, node, sub-family, issue key horty:<sub-family>, outcome (yes = pi), date, number of factors, reason ids, in_factors (1 = has a reason, so it is in factors.tsv), reader, family.
factors.v1.tsv, factor_vocab.v1.tsv, factor_cases.v1.tsv10,123 / 233 / 2,399v1, superseded: 32% factor precision.
factors_work/factor_quotes.tsv444Supporting quote for every kept factor (an exact substring of the decision text).

Precision, before and after. The first pass was too loose and was replaced. Blind spot-check of the second pass against the first:

measurev295% CIv1
Factor present (precision)37/40 = 0.930.80–0.970.32
Reason flag correct31/35 = 0.890.74–0.950.34
Court decides the question28/30 = 0.930.79–0.980.87
Outcome correct (of decided)28/28 = 1.000.88–1.000.88
Item fully right (decides, outcome, every factor and reason)26/302/30

Consistency. The Lean runner examined 44 binding bases on the real factors: 43 are consistent and 1 is not, horty:preemption_express. An independent Python recomputation of 51 sub-family bases finds 50 consistent and agrees with the runner on all 51. In out/findings.tsv: 43 hortyConsistentBase, 1 inconsistentBindingBase, 1 hortySelfInconsistent. The one inconsistency is a gap in the factor vocabulary, not a conflict in the law: see below.

Why express preemption is inconsistent, and what changed from v1 to v2

Results (factors_work/horty_bases.tsv):

  • 50 of 51 sub-family bases are consistent. Of the 34 non-trivial bases (≥ 2 cases, both outcomes), 33 are consistent.
  • 1 is inconsistent: preemption_express. It has 16 cases and 4 conflicting pairs, all through Aloha Airlines v. Director of Taxation (1983, H6088866.2). Removing that one case makes the base consistent.
  • Why the pairs conflict: gpt-6.1-sol read all 4 pairs (conflict_kinds2.jsonl), and all 4 are coarseVocabulary. The extractions are right, but the factor "exception names state regulatory subject" does not tell an exception that covers the challenged law from one that merely names the subject. Aloha's tax fell outside the saving clause. The pilotage, licensing and safety cases fell inside it.
  • What would fix it: a finer factor, "challenged law falls within the express saving clause" (delta).
  • Conflict breakdown, v1 → v2:
    • extraction error 126 → 0;
    • different question 26 → 0;
    • coarse vocabulary 5 → 4;
    • doctrinal change 2 → 0.
    • v1's two doctrinal-change pairs were Loper Bright against Chevron-era cases. Those cases did not survive the stricter v2 pass.

Limits.

The misses:

  • two single-Justice in-chambers stay opinions read as decisions: California v. Green on remand, and INS v. Legalization Assistance Project;
  • Freeman v. Hewit: a factor stretched to fit, and the Court rested on the direct-tax rule instead;
  • Mullenix: high-speed flight was present, but the Court relied on other facts.

Fix still open: exclude in-chambers opinions, using decisions2 form or the "Circuit Justice" heading.

Reading:

  • v2 factors and reasons are usable as data. They stay tag U (model reading), never a premise.
  • The remaining inconsistency is a vocabulary gap, not extraction noise.
  • Recall is now the limit: 1,333 decided cases fit no sub-family. A next pass would add sub-families for the biggest gaps (general content-based speech, Chevron statutory merits), then re-run verify2.py on the cases with subfamily = none.

Coverage is the cost: 269 cases against v1's 2,399. 45 sub-families have at least 2 cases, and 34 of those have both outcomes. The largest are miranda_warnings_waiver (19), preemption_express (16), takings_physical (16), dormant_commerce_nondiscriminatory_tax_burdens (23), standing_personal_injury (13) and agency_deference_statutory_merits (11).

The funnel from 2,399 cases read (FACTORS.md)

Funnel:

  • 2,399 cases read.
  • 1,333 matched no sub-family. They mostly decide questions outside the narrowed sub-families, e.g. general content-based speech rules or Chevron step-one statutory merits.
  • 29 were not decided or had an unclear outcome.
  • 683 had no factor present.
  • 85 had factors but no reason.
  • 269 cases enter factors.tsv.
  • 444 factors were kept and 11,738 marked absent.

Cost. 20.36M tokens, $39.94 at assumed list prices, both passes.

8. Vulnerability heatmaps

Calendar heatmaps in the style of the well-known chart of CVE publications by day: one panel per year, a row per weekday, a column per week. No Lean was run for them; they count the outputs above and the earlier US Code work. Definitions, peaks and caveats are in report/heatmaps/HEATMAPS.md; the full-size PNG and SVG files are beside it.

Decisions relying on bad law, by day

Each square is a day; its colour is the number of decisions decided that day that cite, as authority, a decision whose status was already negative in the citing court's chain of authority: overruled or abrogated, vacated or reversed, withdrawn, superseded by statute, or not citable. These are the Lean findings citesOverruled, citesVacated, citesWithdrawn, citesNotCitable and appliesSupersededHolding, counted once per citing decision. 49,541 decisions in 1990–2019: 24,103 cite an overruled decision, 21,565 a vacated or reversed one, 4,009 a withdrawn one, 1,223 one that is not citable and 0 a superseded holding (kinds overlap; the last needs a conduct date the data do not carry). The busiest day was Friday 30 June 2000 (27), an end-of-term release day. Dates that carry only a month or a year (the 1st of a month in court-years where the 1st is far over-represented, and every 1 January) are dropped; weekends are nearly empty, as in the CVE original. Not-citable citations are not always improper, so that part over-counts.

Precedent broken, by day

Each square counts the admitted negative status events dated that day: a later decision with power over the target overrules, abrogates, reverses, vacates or withdraws it (one event per witness row of a negativeAdmitted row in out/status.tsv, dated by the treating decision). 12,597 events in 1990–2019: 66% same-case reversals and vacaturs and 31% overrulings; the busiest day was Wednesday 14 February 1996 (14). The certificate checker passes more negative treatments than this; only the ones the run gave effect are counted. Coverage thins after mid-2019.

US Code vulnerabilities introduced, by day

The same chart for the Code, from the record of every section version since 1995. A day's count adds three kinds of defect: explicit cross-references that start to dangle (broken by a later law or edition, or written so; held-out audit 68% real), amending instructions of laws since 2013 whose struck words are not in the section (the one failure class the audit found mostly real, though most are the Code's editorial wording rather than drafting errors), and duplicate designations among siblings. 8,212 defects in 1995–2026; the peak, Friday 19 December 2014 (817), is the enactment of title 54 (Pub. L. 113-287), which moved the National Park Service laws out of title 16. Edition releases show as single heavy days, and before 2017 the record dates changes on enactment.

Source: caselaw-lean-2/report/heatmaps/heatmaps.json · caselaw-lean-2/report/heatmaps/HEATMAPS.md · caselaw-lean-2/report/heatmaps/series.json

9. Loopholes and mistakes found (the hunt)

5 patterns of mistake were searched for over the corpus, and the rule tables were searched for loopholes. Each pattern first had to recreate known mistakes; it was then run over the corpus, and a sample of what it reported was read blind by Claude subagents, who saw the decision text and not the first reader's verdict.

The hunt searched the run before the fixes it led to. Counts in this section are those of that run; section 7 has the final run. The last part of this section says what changed.

Per pattern

1 zombie precedent73,568est. 1,815-4,18419/22 = 86% (67-95%), two readers; first reader alone 4/20 and 4/1021/42 literature overrulings marked negative (50%); 0/3 later-court call-outs30
2 unpublished as binding2,880375, then 20/20 (0-16%); refined 1/2known case cites a decision not in the corpus1
3 panel overrules panel1,869409, then 5814/22 = 64% (43-80%), two readers; first reader alone 2/200/2 (second read against audit-confirmed)18
4 two-date error13,60526 (runner), 2 (reader)runner 0/20 (0-16%); reader 1/2; unsettled candidates 2/24runner's 26 are not instances3
5 losing side after resolution6,50635 of 725 read6/20 = 30% (15-52%); top list 6/12164/304 losing-side labels confirmed by later courts (54%)12
6 rulesrule tablessee belownot a sample--

Audit intervals are Wilson 95%. "Recall on known" is the share of known mistakes the pattern recreates. Pattern 6 is a search of the rule tables, not a sample.

Readers and audit design (HUNT.md)

As in the tax-code loophole work: recreate known mistakes, run the validated pattern, blind-audit.

  • Candidates come from the runner (out/findings.tsv, out/status.tsv, out/splits.tsv), the gold tables and the citation edges. The citing passage (± 900 characters around each citation) is read from the git objects.
  • Readers. Two, labelled in every work/*_out.jsonl row (model):
    • azure gpt-5.4-mini: the first pass before the hand-over (pattern 1: 5,389 rows; pattern 2: 1,598; pattern 3: 1,860; split sides: 394). Kept, not extended.
    • claude-subagent: everything after (pattern 2 remainder 602, pattern 4 all 799, pattern 5 all 725, second reads of patterns 1, 2 and 3: 466 + 256 + 409) and every audit. No external model was called after the hand-over.
  • Blind audit. Per pattern, about 20 reported instances at random, the candidates for the top list, and decoys the pattern did not report, shuffled, 7 per auditor. The auditor gets the decision text (the negating decision's own passage for pattern 1), not the first reader's verdict, and answers limb by limb. Intervals are Wilson 95%. No decoy was confirmed in patterns 1, 2, 4 and 5 (0 of 42); pattern 3 is the exception (below).
  • What the audits changed. The first reader was too generous in patterns 1 and 3. A second read with the negating court's words (pattern 1) and the judges line and circulation footnotes (pattern 3) raised precision from 20-40% to 86% and from 10% to 64%. Both precisions are reported; the second is the pattern's.

The strongest findings

Zombie precedent: courts applying overruled law

Candidates 73,568; reported est. 1,815-4,184; audit precision 19/22 = 86% (67-95%), two readers; first reader alone 4/20 and 4/10; confirmed 30.

  1. In re Odyssey Healthcare, 310 S.W.3d 419 (Tex. 2010) ← National League of Cities v. Usery, 426 U.S. 833: applies its "traditional governmental functions" test; Garcia (1985) overruled it and is not cited.
  2. United States v. Helsey, 463 F. Supp. 1111 (D. Mont. 1979) ← Hammer v. Dagenhart, 247 U.S. 251: quoted as authority to hold a federal statute beyond Congress's power; overruled by Darby (1941).
  3. State v. Loudon, 857 S.W.2d 878 (Tenn. Crim. App. 1993) ← Minersville v. Gobitis, 310 U.S. 586: quoted as the Court's view on religious exemptions; overruled by Barnette (1943).
  4. International Ass'n of Machinists v. Sandsberry, 277 S.W.2d 776 (Tex. Civ. App. 1954) ← Grovey v. Townsend, 295 U.S. 45: cited for no state action; overruled on that by Smith v. Allwright (1944).
More: the predicate, the known cases, the corpus run, the audit and all 10 listed instances

Predicate (Hunt.zombie): the status of the cited issue on the citing date is overruled, abrogated, reversed, vacated or withdrawn; the citing court relies on it for the negated proposition; it does not note the history; it is not the same case. Every instance is a citesOverruled, citesVacated or citesWithdrawn finding (zombie_is_spec_finding).

Known cases. 42 overrulings from the CRS table and casebooks (data/known_overrulings.tsv): all 42 targets resolve; the status layer marks 21 negative from the right date (50%, 36-65%) and 3 more as partly negative. The 18 it misses are partial or implicit overrulings (Plessy, Lochner, Swift v. Tyson, Wolf, Ohio v. Roberts, Conley) and overrulers after the corpus ends (Dobbs, Loper Bright). For the 21, every later citer is a finding. Later courts' own call-outs ("the court below relied on X, which had been overruled"): 146 notes, 3 resolvable instances, none in the findings (the targets carry a partial status). The first reader called 3 of 20 such known citations zombies. So recall is bounded by the status layer, about one half.

Corpus. 38,778 citesOverruled + 36,020 citesVacated findings; 73,568 with metadata; citation located in 71,919. Silent citations (no history word, negating decision not cited): 16,718 overruled, 11,110 reversed/vacated. First reader on a weighted sample of 5,389: 50% and 57% of silent citations called zombies. Second reader confirms 12% (30/250) and 17.5% (21/120) of those. Estimated true instances: 1,815 counting only what both readers accept (a lower figure: the second reader rejected 6 of 11 instances the audit confirmed) to 4,184 (first reader × audit precision).

Audit. First reader alone: overruled 4/20 (8-42%), reversed/vacated 4/10 (17-69%). The usual failure (15 of the 16 rejected): the decision was overruled on another point. Both readers: 19/22 (67-95%). Decoys 0/14.

Predicates. Hunt.inconsistentBase (Horty, pair form: opposite outcomes, each reason present in the other's facts); Hunt.persistingSplit (Spec.split); Hunt.losingSideAfterResolution.

Horty. 354 Supreme Court holdings with factors in 53 question families: 4 conflicting pairs, all in express pre-emption (data/p5_horty.tsv). Aloha Airlines v. Director of Taxation (1983) holds the state tax pre-empted because the clause names the regulated transaction, with a state-authority exception present; Anderson v. Pacific Coast S.S. (1912), City of Columbus v. Ours Garage (2002), Chamber of Commerce v. Whiting (2011) and one 2026 decision give the exception priority with the same two factors present. At this factor grain the base binding every federal court orders the two reasons both ways. The other 52 families are consistent. The factor vocabulary is coarse (about one factor per case), so this is a lead, not a holding.

Persisting splits. out/splits.tsv: 335 split rows (opposite good-law answers by circuits that do not bind each other; 123 under Title 18, 80 under Title 8, 56 under Title 28) and 139 conflict rows (one court bound by both answers). Not audited. Spot check: several are stale because the resolving Supreme Court holding is not in holdings.tsv (Wideman v. Burger on Title VII retaliation, resolved by Burlington Northern v. White; Banuelos-Galviz v. Garcia-Romo, resolved by Niz-Chavez).

Loopholes in the rules of precedent

Found by running the reference engine (ref/precedent_ref.py) over the rule tables and counting the decisions each combination touches (p6_rules.py, p6_more.py; data/p6*.tsv). These are properties of the rules as we model them; each names the doctrine it rests on.

b. Successor-court gaps (Hunt.orphaned, Hunt.cutoffWindow). 37 successions.

  • New Jersey 1948. The Court of Errors and Appeals binds the new trial and appellate courts. The old Supreme Court (an intermediate court, 21,129 decisions) has no adoption row: persuasive on the new Supreme Court and on the Appellate Division, binding (absent conflict) only on trial courts.
  • D.C. 1971 (M.A.P. v. Ryan). A D.C. Circuit decision of 29 Jan 1971 binds the D.C. trial courts; one of 2 Feb 1971 is persuasive. On the D.C. Court of Appeals itself the engine gives "strongly persuasive" (a court of last resort is not bound by itself), although M.A.P. binds its divisions: a gap in our rule, not in the law.
  • Kentucky 1976. No gap: the old Court of Appeals binds the new one and every circuit court.
  • Tenth Circuit 1929. The same kind of split as 1981, the opposite answer: 7,364 Eighth Circuit decisions bind nobody in the Tenth (18,141 later citations there).
  • Court of Claims 1982. 17,104 decisions carry "unknown" force on the Federal Circuit, because South Corp. excludes trial-division decisions and the data cannot separate them.
  • Without any binding successor: Kansas Court of Appeals 1895-1901 (1,744 decisions), Court of Appeals of Indian Territory (574), New Jersey Court of Chancery (10,882). Five old courts, 37,668 decisions, 68,680 later citations.

c. Dual high courts (Hunt.dualHighCourtConflict). Texas and Oklahoma: both courts bind the intermediate courts and neither has power over the other. 8 treatments cross the line (Texas 4, Oklahoma 4), 7 styled "overruled", for example Jackson v. State, 548 S.W.2d 685 (Tex. Crim. App. 1977) on State v. Olsen, 360 S.W.2d 398 (Tex. 1962). All have power "no" (H2.dualLastResort), so status never changes and an intermediate court is bound by both.

e. Adoption chains carrying overruled law (Hunt.adoptionCarriesOverruled). 48 overrulings of pre-split decisions by one heir: the Fifth Circuit en banc overruled 37 old-Fifth decisions that still bind the Eleventh (63 later Eleventh Circuit citations); the Eleventh overruled 8 that still bind the Fifth (30); D.C. 3 (5). Example: United States v. Salinas, 654 F.2d 319 (5th Cir. Aug 1981), overruled by United States v. Adamson, 700 F.2d 953 (5th Cir. 1983) (en banc), cited 11 times since by the Eleventh Circuit. Our Spec gets this wrong: status is global (Spec.citesOverruled: "not relative to the citing court"), so the runner reports 25 of these 98 citations as citing overruled law. Status after an adoption cut should be per heir.

More: forum choice, unpublished-opinion windows, commission opinions

a. Forum choice. A holding binds in one forum and not its sibling (Hunt.forumDependent).

  • Federal law in state court: 50 systems treat their circuit as persuasive, 4 as binding, 2 as strongly persuasive. The same circuit holding binds the federal district court and not the state court across the street.
  • State trial courts: 36 systems statewide, 3 choose on conflict, 3 own-district-then-any (Florida, Illinois), 3 own-district only. Under the Florida and Illinois rule one district's panel binds every trial court in the state until the home district speaks, while it does not bind the other districts' appellate courts.
  • 1,442 treatments in which a court declines to follow or "overrules" a court of another system (670 state-state, 527 state courts on federal courts, 245 federal on state); none has power, so both answers stand.
  • 13 systems have a first-in-time rule; the rest let the later panel prevail in practice.

d. Unpublished-opinion windows. 40 windows (data/p6d_unpublished_windows.tsv). The 49 Fifth Circuit unpublished decisions before 1996 are precedent there, and those before Oct 1981 also bind the Eleventh Circuit, whose own unpublished opinions never bind; 41 later ones bind the Fifth and are persuasive in the Eleventh. 600 Texas civil appeals decisions are binding though unpublished. Territorial adopters (Guam, the Northern Marianas, the Virgin Islands) inherit 69,218 and 15,149 Ninth and Third Circuit unpublished decisions as persuasive.

f. Commission opinions (Hunt.commissionForce). The notation decides: "opinion adopted" binds as the Supreme Court's own, "judgment adopted" is result only, none is persuasive. Of 4,676 Texas Commission of Appeals decisions only 955 carry a notation row (945 "opinion adopted"); the other 3,721 fall to the default. On lower courts the engine gives the probe (a 1943 Commission decision) full vertical force (binding:H1): the notation limits only the adopter. 7,004 Missouri and 3,242 Texas criminal commissioner opinions are typed "other" or "opinion approved" and treated as the court's own.
