The hunt fixes in the Lean (DEVIATIONS.md 68–73)
  1. Divisions of a court of last resort (H6, §3.2/§4 DC; M.A.P. v. Ryan, 285 A.2d 310 (D.C. 1971)). A court of last resort with a court-level horizontal row (system = -court_id) is read as sitting in divisions. A division is bound by the court's own decisions as that row says (divisionRelation, forceDiv), and only an en banc–equivalent bench overrules them (lastResortBench). The court itself, en banc, is still not bound (relation's H1self), so nothing_binds_last_resort holds as locked: it speaks of the court, not of a division. Every force the runner computes is for the court as it ordinarily sits (forceDiv); forceDiv_eq_force proves this changes nothing for any court that is not a court of last resort. A system-level row does not make a court of last resort a divisional court. Decisions of the court's earlier, intermediate era fall to the higher-court rule (any bench), on both sides.
  2. Status after an adoption cut-off is per heir (H4, F10; Reach, reachOf, inLine, statusFor). Heirs are binding adoptions with filter all or unitB; persuasive adoptions and notation filters make none. A status-changing treatment reaches: every line if it is SCOTUS's; the original line if it is by the decision's own court, a court that replaced it (a succession other than a split), a higher court of its system, or an adopter once the original court has no epoch; an heir if the treating court is that heir, or stands above it, or the original line overruled on or before the heir's cut-off. A citing court is in an heir's line when it is the heir or a court below it (same system, lower tier; under a federal court of appeals, its circuit). Limits: (a) court epochs in courts2.tsv rarely end, so "the original court is gone" almost never fires: after a split that ended the old court (Alabama 1969), a successor's overruling reaches only its own line; (b) per-heir status is applied to the citation findings (cites*, citesLaterNegated, supersededConductUnknown) only. status.tsv, the treatment-level families, splits, conflicts and Horty bases still read the union status (negative if negative in any line).
  3. Superseded holdings need a conduct date and a holding-level match (H2, §7 AB1). SCHEMA carries no conduct date for a citing decision, and its own date is not one. appliesSupersededHolding therefore needs statusAtConduct = some … and is never emitted from the present data. The low-confidence family atRisk supersededConductUnknown:<issue> is emitted instead when (a) the cited holding is superseded for the latest conduct the citing decision could concern (its own date), and (b) the citing decision has a holding on the same issue, or on an issue whose US Code block is the block the superseding law rewrote. The old fallback (a citing decision with no holdings citing a decision all of whose holdings are negative) does not apply to it.
  4. Panel departures (H3b, F7). panelDepartsWithoutEnBanc needs a bench known to be a panel or a division (an unknown bench and an opinion circulated to the full court make no finding, whatever the circulation rule), and a strong or within-unit rule covering both the precedent's date and the treating date. A missing row makes no finding. A federal court of appeals makes none before 1 September 1948 (enBancStatuteDate, 28 U.S.C. § 46(c); tag L). Power is unchanged (a missing row still needs an en banc bench, R31), so status is unchanged. horizontal rows stay keyed by the precedent's date: dating a rule's start also ends the binding force of older decisions on the court's own panels, which is why the federal date is a constant and not a row date. Ohio (soft before 1 July 2010) and Louisiana (within-circuit from 1997) are dated in system_rules.tsv (tools/caselaw2/rule_dates_fix.py); those two dates are from memory (tag L) and need the courts agent's check.
  5. Texas notations that add no approval (a, sweep seed 51925). writPromotes now also excludes "denied", "dism.", "w.o.j." and the criminal "PDR" wordings, as the reference does.
  6. Closed (c): a split successor without a firm adoption row (round 2). Reading, on both sides: a split succession row never by itself makes the new court hold the old court's decisions. Only an adoption row does, and each run (all tables; S/L tables) reads its own adoption rows. rename, replace and absorb rows are unchanged. Grounds: a court made by dividing another does not take the old court's precedent by the division alone. The Eleventh Circuit took the former Fifth's by its own en banc decision (Bonner v. City of Prichard, 661 F.2d 1206, 1209 (11th Cir. 1981)); the Tenth Circuit, made from the Eighth in 1929, did not take the Eighth's (Estate of McMorris, 243 F.3d 1254, 1258 (10th Cir. 2001); doctrine F10). Alabama, Act No. 987 of 1969 (eff. 1 Oct 1969):
    • the Court of Appeals continued as the Court of Criminal Appeals (same court, same three judges): Coalite, Inc. v. Aldridge (Ala. Civ. App. 1969) says the case "was transferred from the Court of Appeals, now the Court of Criminal Appeals, to this, the Court of Civil Appeals, on October 1, 1969, pursuant to Act 987". A continued court holds its own decisions (H3). The court acts on that footing: "We overrule Willis, supra, so far as it might restrain us from acting ex mero motu" (Ala. Crim. App., 17 Aug 1971, node 110729, of a 1964 Court of Appeals decision). The adoption row 3 <- 1 is therefore verified and its tag moved U to S in data/adoption.tsv (round 2, one row; the original is adoption.pre_round2.tsv);
    • the Court of Civil Appeals was a new court. No decision or statute adopting the old court's decisions as its own was found in four searches. Its practice treats them as its precedent (it overruled Colquitt, a 1964 Court of Appeals decision, in 2007, node 106047), but that is practice, not an adoption shown. The row 2 <- 1 stays U, so findings that rest on it are firm = 0 on both sides. The Lean already read inheritance only from adoption rows. The reference's firm run let the successor hold the old court's decisions through the S-tagged succession row; it now reads a split as the Lean does. Expected on the 11 real firm flags: the 10 Court of Criminal Appeals keys become firm on both sides (data), the 1 Court of Civil Appeals key becomes not firm on both sides (reading).
The hunt fixes in differential testing (DIFFTEST.md §8.3)

Made in the Lean (LEAN.md "Hunt fixes", DEVIATIONS 68–71) and, by a separate agent from the written reading, in the reference (REF_NOTES "Revisions: hunt fixes"): H2 (appliesSupersededHolding needs a conduct date and a holding-level match; atRisk supersededConductUnknown instead), H3b (a known panel, a rule in force on both dates, no federal finding before 1 Sept 1948), H4 (status after an adoption cut-off per heir, on the citation findings), H6 (divisions). The generator gained a hunt layer on its own random stream (gen.py, --no-hunt reproduces old universes): D.C. Circuit / D.C. Court of Appeals / Ohio courts, a binding adoption with a cut-off, overrulings by the source court, the adopter and SCOTUS with citers from every line, benches of every kind around dated rule rows, and supersessions with citers on the same issue, the same US Code block, another issue or none.

The first sweep with that layer (seeds 52000–52999) disagreed in 86 universes (status 103/117,265, findings 234/54,988, splits 56/18,873, conflicts 106/7,118). Three classes, all about a court of last resort that holds decisions by adoption:

ClassTriageFix
A court of last resort (no court-level row) overruling a decision it adopted: the Lean asked for an en banc bench, the reference let any bench (H1)(a)adoptedLastResortBench: free unless the court sits in divisions
The divisional row for an adopted decision keyed on the precedent's date: M.A.P. binds the divisions to pre-1971 D.C. Circuit decisions, which a row dated 1971 does not cover(c), both sidesKeyed on the question or treating date for adopted decisions
Conflict displacement: "a decision held by binding adoption is displaced only by a holding that also binds its adopter" applied at a court outside the adopter's line (a California Supreme Court holding could not displace a D.C. Circuit reading of California law at the federal district court)(b), and the Lean reached the right answer only through precedenceb4: only an adopter in whose line the destination stands (both sides)

After these: 300 universes (52000–52299) 0 disagreements but the b4 class (5 universes), then the final sweep below.

The predicates in Lean

LegalProofs/CaseLaw2/Hunt.lean: 14 theorems and 44 #guard checks on the cases named here and on near misses. It is imported by Core.lean, so its theorems are in the registry of section 5.

Limits

  • Passage readers see ± 900 characters; audits see up to 34,000 characters of the citing opinion. Where an auditor relied on memory for the negating decision, the explanation says so.
  • Audit samples are 20-22 per pattern; intervals are wide. Pattern 2 (refined) and pattern 4 have 2 and 3 instances.
  • Pattern 1 and 3 first reads are Azure; second reads and audits are Claude. Patterns 4 and 5 have one Claude read.
  • Estimates are for the candidate pools named, not for all US case law. Pattern 1 cannot see overrulings the status layer misses; pattern 5 covers only splits whose losing side the Court named; pattern 4 only the 36 listed overrides.
  • Persisting splits and the Horty result are unaudited.
  • The second reads have low recall (pattern 1: 5 of 11; pattern 3: 0 of 2), so the two-reader counts are floors.

Why we find only about half of the overrulings on the published lists

The Supreme Court Database flags 278 decisions as altering precedent. After four rounds we find 141 of them. That looks low for something as public as the Supreme Court overruling itself. It is low for four reasons, and only one of them is our reader being weak.

1. Most overrulings do not say “overruled”. A court rarely writes “we overrule X”. It writes that X “is no longer good law”, that it “cannot be reconciled with our later cases”, that “we decline to follow it”, that its reasoning “has been eroded”, or it simply decides the other way and leaves readers to draw the conclusion. Brown v. Board of Education never says it overrules Plessy; it says “any language in Plessy contrary to this finding is rejected”. We diagnosed every miss at the start of round 2 by reading the overruling decision. Of 196 flagged decisions we then missed, 66 (a third) had no overruling words at all: in most the earlier case is discussed and departed from without a word of overruling; in some only the dissent or the syllabus says the Court overruled it; in some the earlier case is not even cited. The database’s coders, and the Constitution Annotated’s editors, are making a legal judgment that the later case is inconsistent with the earlier one. Our model is built not to make that judgment: a decision’s status changes only when a court with the power to change it says so in words we can quote. An implicit overruling shows in our output as “at risk”, never as “overruled”. Round 4 added a tier for the case where a later decision of a court with standing says so in words (“X, overruled by Y”): 8 of these 66 decisions now carry such an “at risk” row naming them as the overruling decision (11 of the 101 Constitution Annotated pairs), among them Brown for Plessy, Mapp for Wolf and Crawford for Ohio v. Roberts. None of them changes a status.

2. The words vary more than any list of patterns. Another 110 of the 196 misses were filtered out before a model ever read them. The largest group (126 across all gold sets) used a wording none of our scan patterns covered. These are real ones from the misses: “we are not satisfied that those decisions are founded on a correct view of the law”; “must be regarded as having been distinctly overthrown”; “we cannot adopt that decision or apply its principles”; “they can no longer be guiding”; “to the extent that what the Court now says is inconsistent with what was said in Miles v. Graham, the latter cannot survive”; “we therefore reject as untenable the diversities taken in the St. Louis Trust cases”. Each is unmistakable to a lawyer and each is a new sentence to a pattern. Others were dropped because the sentence did not look like the court’s own act (it was in the passive, or it described the rule rather than the case), or because our map of the opinion put the sentence in a concurrence when it was in the opinion of the court. Recent slip opinions were hard-wrapped, which broke sentence splitting; that is why Dobbs, Wayfair and Loper Bright were missing until round 3. This is the part that further work fixes, and it is where the gain from 29.5% to 50.7% came from.

3. Naming the target is its own problem. In 11 of the 196 the court does say it overrules something, but we could not tie the words to a decision: “the rule of the Slaughter-House line of cases”, “our decision in that case”, a case named only by one party, or a citation to a reporter page that holds several decisions. A certificate needs the target to resolve to exactly one decision. When it does not, we admit nothing.

4. The lists and we count different things. The database flags a decision that altered precedent; it does not say which precedent, so a match needs us to admit an overruling by that decision of some Supreme Court case. The lists also include partial overrulings (“overruled insofar as…”), which we record against one holding, and overrulings of a line of cases. And they are not complete in the other direction: of 12 Supreme Court overrulings we admit that the database does not flag, a blind reading found 11 are real.

Source: round2/recall.md and round2/recall_misses.tsv. Rounds 2 and 3 then recovered 59 of the 196 database misses, almost all from the second row. The first row is the floor: about a quarter of the 278 flagged decisions cannot be found by any reader that requires the overruling court’s own words.

So the honest reading of 50.7% is this. Of the overrulings a court actually announces in words, we now find most. Of the overrulings lawyers recognise, about a quarter to a third were never announced, and a formal model that will not infer them will not find them. We think that is the right side to err on. Precision is 92.8%: when the model says the Supreme Court overruled a case, it almost always did, and it can show the sentence.

Why agreement with later courts’ notes is lower still

When a later court cites a case it often adds a note: “X, overruled by Y”, “abrogated by Y”, “overruled on other grounds by Y”. We hold 193,411 such notes back as a test. Our model agrees with about 28% of the “overruled” notes that name the overruling decision. Three things explain most of the gap, and they are not the same as above.

1. A note is a later court’s opinion about Y, not what Y said. We had readers open the named decision Y for 120 notes, blind. In only 44 (37%) does Y’s majority say in words that it overrules, abrogates or disapproves X. In 13 it rejects X’s holding without saying so; in 38 it only mentions X or reports what another court did; in 25 X is not discussed in the passages at all. For “abrogated by” the figure is 4 of 34: abrogation is almost always a later court’s inference that a higher court’s ruling left an earlier case untenable. A model that requires Y’s own words can agree with at most about 37% of notes, and with very few abrogation notes. That is the main ceiling.

2. Most notes say “on other grounds”. Of 15,768 “overruled” notes that name the overruling decision, 10,406 say the case was overruled on other grounds, and 1,434 say in part. The citing court is telling its reader that the point it cites the case for survives. Our model tracks that: it records the overruling against one holding and leaves the rest of the decision good. Counting those notes as “the decision is overruled” and asking whether we agree mixes two different questions. Where a note names the overruling decision and we have admitted an overruling of the same case, we name the same decision about 82% of the time.

3. Notes are written by busy courts and read by patterns. A blind check of our own reading of the notes found 84% had the target, the overruling decision and the kind all right; the rest were our misreadings, such as taking a case in a parenthetical for the target. Notes also repeat one another: a wrong “overruled by” in one opinion is copied into the next. In v1 we found that a third of the decisions courts credit with overruling a case never say they overrule it. The notes are the best independent evidence we have, but they are a noisy witness. Commercial citators have the same problem: the study cited in our design research found that each missed or mislabelled about a third of negative treatments.

4. The rest is the same as above: wordings we do not scan for, targets we cannot resolve, and, for lower courts, overruling decisions that are not in the corpus or are unpublished orders.

Put together: the note test measures two things at once, whether our reader finds what the overruling court wrote, and whether later courts describe that court accurately. On the first, where both can be checked, we name the same overruling decision 82% of the time. The second is not ours to fix, and is one of the findings of this work: a large share of what courts call an overruling was never stated by the court that is said to have done it.

Blind audits

Key finding: later courts' notes are a noisy target. We drew 120 named negative notes and had blind readers check whether the named decision's own majority says it. It says it in words in 44 (37%, Wilson 29–46%). It rejects the holding without saying so in 13, only mentions or reports it in 38, and the target is absent from the excerpts in 25. For abrogation the gap is widest: 4 of 34 abrogation notes are stated by the named decision; abrogation is mostly a later court's judgment. For overruling, 35 of 72. A model that admits only what a court says itself cannot agree with a note whose named decision never says it. So agreement with notes understates how often the model is right, and the blind audits, not the notes, measure precision.

Of the ≈ 71 classes:

  • the Lean was wrong in 26 (37%);
  • the reference in 17 (24%);
  • 24 (34%) were open points of doctrine, now settled one way on both sides;
  • 4 (6%) were data or contract problems.

The Lean errors were mostly in the unverified glue (Run.lean: ids, segmentation, admission, findings, splits, firm), 15 of 26. The other 11 were in the trusted Spec:

  • canChangeStatus: trial self-power, appellate divisions, adoption, the Federal Circuit;
  • fedHier: F11(b);
  • relation: E3;
  • histEffect / lapseOfDecision: reinstatement and revival;
  • supersession scope;
  • formCap: HD6;
  • horizontalForce: units.

In every case the change stayed inside the existing theorem statements. Two proofs (no_overrule_of_binding_superior and only_scotus_changes_scotus) needed one extra simp hypothesis.

Each universe has 60 decisions (120 in the stress sweep) and is generated by gen.py. It contains:

  • every court family: SCOTUS, circuits with a split and adoption, the Federal Circuit, CFC, the Tax Court, Maine, California with units, Kentucky epochs, and the Texas dual high courts;
  • dated S/L/U rules;
  • every treatment, history, scope and temporal kind;
  • corrupted certificates;
  • supersessions, including retroactive_to = 1 (added for the new SCHEMA convention);
  • reviewGrantedForce rows (added).

Run: python gen.py --seed S --rounds N [--n 60] --out DIR --ref --lean --diff (8 at a time, compiled runner).

Residuals

  • Generated data, final sweep (seeds 20000–24999): 5,000 rounds, 0 with a disagreement (status 0/316,963, findings 0/51,793, certs 0/465,023, splits 0/48,107 keys).
  • Stress sweep (n = 120, seeds 30000–31999): 2,000 rounds, 1 with a disagreement: two firm-only differences on cites:vacated (seed 30984), and no verdict differences (status 0/253,453, findings 2/40,926 firm only, certs 0/372,157, splits 0/70,483).
  • Regression set: fixtures/regress/, 110 universes. These are the 40 original counterexamples, plus the generator seeds behind every class triaged after the first iterations. python regress.py passes: 110 universes, 0 disagreeing.
  • Fixtures: status 0/14, findings 0/3, certs 0/13, splits 0/1 (2 reason-only cert differences: Lean disqualified against reference noTarget, both rejecting).

The one open residual, seed 30984 (n = 120), is a firm flag only. The finding is the same on both sides. The cited decision is wholly vacated under all the tables, but under the S/L-only tables (with a U-tagged en banc row removed) only through its single holding. The reference's firm run reaches the same finding through the "all holdings negative" route and marks it firm. The Lean computes the firm flag of the whole-decision row only from the whole-decision status, so it marks it not firm. Triage: (c), a convention: is a finding firm when the S/L tables reach the same finding by another route? Not yet unified, because it occurred in 1 of 57,000 universes. The reference's reading is the natural one; the fix belongs in the Lean glue.

Uncompared kinds (only one side defines them) are not residuals, but they are coverage gaps for the reference:

  • Lean ignoresBindingInUnit and atRisk:citesLaterNegated;
  • reference atRisk:soft/claim/contraryBinding;
  • Lean conflict split rows.

Triage of the final residual

All 45 remaining rows were triaged, a census rather than a sample; difftest/real11/sample.tsv holds all of them. The 100-row stratified samples of real4–real9 (difftest/real*/sample.tsv) are what drove the fixes above. Every class in them was resolved, so they leave no residual.

  • 40 of 45: one pattern, D.C. Court of Appeals decisions from its intermediate era (1963–1971, a U-tagged epoch) treated by the same court after it became the court of last resort (1 Feb 1971). It covers 16 status, 17 + 7 panelDepartsWithoutEnBanc and part of the cites rows.
    • The Lean reads the later court-of-last-resort bench as a higher court of the system, so the overruling is admitted.
    • The reference reads the same court id at another tier as "the same court" for the panel-departure test, and finds a panel departure under the court-level strong row (M.A.P. v. Ryan).
    • Triage: (c), open. Can a court overrule its own pre-promotion decisions with a panel? M.A.P. bears on D.C. Circuit precedent, not on this case. Left unresolved; it needs a doctrine decision.
  • 5 of 45: citation findings that follow from statuses in the same pattern (2 + 1 + 1), and one none/negative vacated row from the same D.C. epoch overlap: (c), same pattern.
Data notes for the agents (d)
  • d5. The reader rewrites data/ in place, so consumers must snapshot.
  • d6. Holdings windows. holdings_cert_text.tsv has start0/end0 equal to the quote's span, but the window text is the ±400-character context. 127,941 of 131,422 holdings therefore fail their certificate on both sides (the 3,481 that pass also have a well-formed window in cert_text.tsv). SCHEMA says the window is the text from start0 to end0. The holdings agent should write start0 = start − 400 (clamped) and end0 = end + 400, or trim the text. Until then, holdings, and with them splits, are almost empty on the real data.
  • d2 and d3 (no reviewGrantedForce rows; no D.C. court-level horizontal row) still stand.

Fuzzing the glue

The TSV parsers and writers are not proved, so they were fuzzed: generated data files, broken in typed ways, loaded by the Lean and by the reference and compared with an oracle that reads SCHEMA literally.

Verification (12 Nov, evening). Windows Application Control blocks the Windows Lean toolchain, so the fixes were compiled and run under Linux Lean 4.35.0 in WSL Ubuntu (run_lean_wsl.sh; LEAN.md "Running under WSL"). The 5,000 cases of seed 7 were regenerated inside WSL and run through the Lean dumper (two passes), the runner's main and the reference: P1–P4 have 0 failures, and P5 has only the documented 64-bit deviation (8 cases; FUZZ.md run B). No new Lean or reference bug was found. One unrelated compile error surfaced: Run.lean read factor_cases.tsv as 10 columns; the file has 11 (fixed).

The fixes in Tsv.lean and the reference (FUZZ.md)

Tsv.lean (fuzz agent's file):

  1. Extra columns accepted. loadRows took ≥ minFields fields, so a tab inside a field silently shifted the columns. For example, an issues row with a tab in its label read the label's tail as the domain. Now it requires exactly the schema's count and logs "n fields ≠ k".
  2. Non-SCHEMA numbers accepted. nat?, int? and natD used trimAscii plus String.toNat?, so 1_000 read as 1000 and 12 as 12. ppm? read . as 0 and 1_0.5 as 10.5. Now they accept ASCII digits only (with a leading - for int?).
  3. BOM. A UTF-8 BOM stayed in line 1's first field: a numeric first row was dropped, and a hash or id was silently altered. Now it is stripped.
  4. Extra CRs. chomp dropped one CR only, so with CR CR LF the last field kept a \r (a tag S\r is not S). Now every trailing CR is dropped.
  5. Invalid UTF-8. getLine decoded invalid UTF-8 lossily (U+FFFD) and the row was used. foldLines now reads bytes in 1 MiB chunks, splits on LF only (a lone CR stays data, as before) and validates each line; an invalid line is rejected and logged as invalid UTF-8.

precedent_ref.py (each change marked # fuzz:). With the original reference, run A gave 24 crashes, 380 row-count mismatches and 475 quote-stage disagreements.

  1. Crash on invalid UTF-8. open(encoding='utf-8') raised on the first invalid byte and the whole run stopped. Lines are now read as bytes, and a bad line is rejected and counted.
  2. Lone CR split rows. open(newline='') treated a lone CR as a line end and split the row. Now only LF ends a line.
  3. Silent mis-parsing of rows. Short rows were padded with '' and extra fields kept, so a 15-field treatment or a tab inside a quote was mis-read. Now read_tsv requires exactly the column count, checks the required integer columns, and counts rejected rows in BAD_ROWS.
  4. Data rows skipped. # lines and header-looking lines were skipped, though Lean reads them. They are now data.
  5. Loose numbers. toint and tofloat took 5, +5, 1_000, NBSP, other scripts' digits, nan and 1e5. They are now strict, and tofloat keeps 6 decimals as Lean's ppm does.
  6. decisions2 loading. Fixes:
    • 8 columns had been accepted; now exactly 9 are required;
    • isdigit() accepted ², and int() then crashed; ids are now ASCII digits;
    • negative courts had been accepted;
    • one huge node id grew the arrays without bound; ids at or above CASELAW2_NODES (default 2^27) are now rejected, as Lean rejects ids beyond its node count;
    • an id or date above 2^31 overflowed array('i'); the arrays are now array('q').
  7. CRLF in quotes. norm_quote collapsed CR LF into one space, shifting offsets. It is now one for one, as in SCHEMA and Cert.norm. The window is normalised before slicing, as Lean does.
  8. Unicode lowercasing. str.lower() was used for cues, disqualifiers and evidence: the Kelvin sign became k and U+0130 became i plus U+0307. It now lowercases ASCII only, as Lean's toLower.
  9. NBSP in name evidence. Name evidence was split with split(), which also splits on NBSP. It now splits on ' ', as Lean does.
  10. Rows Lean calls badRow. A treatment or history row naming an unknown kind or temporal value, or a node with no decisions2 row, is now badRow, as in Lean. It had been admitted when only the target's decision was missing, and an empty temporal read as unknown.

The fixtures' reference outputs are unchanged by all of this: certs, status, findings, splits and splits_asof are byte-identical before and after.

Not tested
  • Run.lean's output writers beyond certs and summary. They are exercised, but not compared value by value.
  • Run.lean's edge reader beyond the direct test of FB-L7 (the fuzzer always uses the fixtures' edges).
  • run_lean.sh's node count (FB-L8) end to end with a huge id; the awk line was tested alone.
  • The reader's clean() (FB-R1) inside the reader; it was tested by a direct call.
  • A range check on court, date and unit (the 64-bit deviation): neither side validates that a date is a date.

Source: caselaw-lean-2/FUZZ.md · caselaw-lean-2/FUZZ_BUGS.md

12. Deviations and limits

DEVIATIONS.md lists 86 numbered departures from doctrine.md, plus the fallbacks for unknown data. Every fallback is a named assume* label, so it appears in the rule path of every verdict that used it.

Fallbacks for unknown data

LabelWhenFallbackWhy this direction
assumeHomeDomainholding's domain unknown (incl. the anonymous issue ⊤)the source court's home domain: federal → federalGeneral, state → stateLaw sys (§8.2)the only way to run before issue extraction
assumePublishedpublication unknownpublishedan unknown channel is usually the official reporter
assumeFullFormform unknownfull opinion
assumeUnpubPersuasiveunpublished, no unpubForce rowpersuasiveFRAP 32.1 default
assumeHorizontalSoftno horizontal row, forcesoft (persuasiveStrong)does not claim a binding force the tables don't give
assumeStrongForPowerno horizontal row, powerstrong (en banc needed)does not admit an overruling the tables don't support
assumeStatewideno trialScope rowstatewidethe majority rule (§4.3)
assumePanelbench unknown, powerpanelconservative
assumeRetroactivetreatment temporal unknownretroactive (Harper)TM2 default for federal law

horizontal uses one fallback for force and the opposite one for power. Both are the conservative direction for what they decide.

The departures that matter most

Selected for this report: those that change what a verdict can say (case kind, pre-Erie, Marks, implicit abrogation, revival, partial scope, certificate targets, splits).

  1. Case kind. Civil vs criminal is not modelled (no column).
    • The dual courts of last resort (TX, OK, H2) each bind every lower court of their system.
    • Two different last-resort courts of one system never bind each other (H2dual).
  2. Swift era (E1). Before 25 Apr 1938, federal decisions on state law are persuasive in federal courts. The Swift "local law" exception (binding) is not modelled, since local and general law cannot be told apart.
  3. Marks (F6). A plurality holding with no marks.tsv row is persuasive. The doctrine's separate grade resultOnly (binding on the result only) is folded into persuasive.
  4. Abrogation by intervening higher authority (F14) changes status only when a court states it in an admitted, explicit treatment row.
    • An inferred abrogation (explicit = 0) feeds atRisk only.
    • The split resolver ranks a SCOTUS holding first, but does not derive implicit abrogations of the lower holdings.
  5. Revival (T3). An overruling lapses when the overruling decision is vacated, withdrawn, substituted, or reversed on every issue.
    • Overruling the overruler does not revive automatically, because the later court may adopt a third rule.
  6. "On other grounds" and unknown scope. otherGrounds, partialUnknown and history scope unknown all reach "some issue". For a named holding, and for the anonymous issue ⊤, that is unknown:partialScope, not negative.
  7. Certificates.
    • The target check is the presence of the citation (spacing and case ignored) or of every name token (≥ 3 characters) in the quote or window. Since the five-limits pass, a cite: evidence must also resolve through the citation index to the row's target when cite_index.tsv is supplied (item 64).
    • Window hashes are re-checked in Lean when window_sha.tsv is supplied (item 65).
    • Cue and disqualifier phrases are fixed lists in Certificate.lean.
  8. Splits.
    • Examined at the asOf date.
    • split rows follow DESIGN layer 5 (D4 triage): two holdings on the question with opposite answers, both good law on asOf, by courts (court, unit) neither of which binds the other (force known and below bindingAbsentConflict both ways), with no good-law holding of a non-trial court binding both. This test is in the runner glue; the Spec's resolver-based split and scotus_resolves_split now back only conflict rows.
    • conflict rows: the bound courts are every (court, unit) that holds on the issue, plus one trial court per system/circuit involved. Opposite permissible answers within one bound court are a conflict.
All simplifications (DEVIATIONS.md 1–29)
  1. Case kind. Civil vs criminal is not modelled (no column).
    • The dual courts of last resort (TX, OK, H2) each bind every lower court of their system.
    • Two different last-resort courts of one system never bind each other (H2dual).
  2. Swift era (E1). Before 25 Apr 1938, federal decisions on state law are persuasive in federal courts. The Swift "local law" exception (binding) is not modelled, since local and general law cannot be told apart.
  3. E1 West v. AT&T. Intermediate state decisions are persuasiveStrong in federal courts; state trial decisions are persuasive (King).
  4. Erie predictions. A federal panel's departure from a circuit Erie prediction after a new state-high-court decision is not specially licensed. Power follows the circuit's horizontal rule.
  5. Marks (F6). A plurality holding with no marks.tsv row is persuasive. The doctrine's separate grade resultOnly (binding on the result only) is folded into persuasive.
  6. Summary affirmances (F2) are binding, without the narrow-issue scope.
  7. Equally divided (F5) → none. Memorandum → persuasive.
    • Data (2026-11-12, limit 13): form memorandum now also covers 643,590 short dispositive orders outside SCOTUS (order language in under 1,500 characters of opinion text; SCHEMA has no order value), so they are persuasive rather than assumeFullForm. Oklahoma and Minnesota "MEMORANDUM OPINION"s are full published opinions and are no longer memorandum (limit 10).
    • Not modelled: Georgia "physical precedent" (concurrence-count test), WV memorandum weight, and Tax Court memorandum vs division opinions (except through form = memorandum).
  8. Commission opinions (H4) are not distinguished (no column).
  9. Golsen (F12). Handled only through the optional decisions2_extra.tsv appeal_venue (the bound decision's circuit). Without it, the Tax Court is a national special court.
  10. BAP decisions are persuasive everywhere (F13, contested). A special court's own precedent is persuasiveStrong (F12 stare decisis).
  11. Unit B (F10). The unitB adoption filter matches decisions whose unit is 2; the courts table must mark Unit B decisions that way.
  12. Adoption across systems (M.A.P. v. Ryan, D.C.) is allowed. This is why the Erie theorem is stated "absent adoption"; Examples.lean shows the adoption case.
  13. SCOTUS is not bound by itself (H1self, persuasiveStrong), like every court of last resort. H1self needs the two courts to be in the same system.
  14. AEDPA (only SCOTUS holdings count on federal habeas) is not modelled.
  15. Abrogation by intervening higher authority (F14) changes status only when a court states it in an admitted, explicit treatment row.
    • An inferred abrogation (explicit = 0) feeds atRisk only.
    • The split resolver ranks a SCOTUS holding first, but does not derive implicit abrogations of the lower holdings.
  16. Revival (T3). An overruling lapses when the overruling decision is vacated, withdrawn, substituted, or reversed on every issue.
    • Overruling the overruler does not revive automatically, because the later court may adopt a third rule.
  17. Vacated opinions have no force. The [U] view that some courts cite them as persuasive is not modelled.
  18. Withdrawal takes effect from its date, not ab initio (TM3).
  19. California review granted (S-CA). This is the approved reviewGrantedForce system rule.
    • Its force is ≤ notCitable → status depublished; otherwise status reviewPending (a persuasive cap).
    • The effect lasts until review is dismissed or the case is decided (affirmed, reversed, modified).
    • Not modelled: the 2021 "transfer with directions to vacate" and the 2021 administrative order. No row → a grant has no effect (as with cert. granted elsewhere).
  20. En banc grant (F8). If no enBancGrantVacatesPanel row covers the court, the panel opinion's status is unknown:enBancRuleUnknown, not good law.
  21. Texas writ/pet. refused (S-TX-3) promotes the opinion to last-resort tier for force. Not distinguished: "writ ref'd n.r.e.", which the data must not label writRefused. Data (2026-11-12, limit 9): history.tsv labels writRefused only for the Texas Supreme Court's "writ refused" / "writ ref'd" (1 row); "n.r.e.", "writ denied" and "writ dismissed" are never writRefused. The 2,287 former rows were the Louisiana Supreme Court's "Writ refused." on court-of-appeal judgments (a refusal to review); they are now kind other (src relabel:other(...)), which cannot be certified (item 52) and changes no status.
  22. "On other grounds" and unknown scope. otherGrounds, partialUnknown and history scope unknown all reach "some issue". For a named holding, and for the anonymous issue ⊤, that is unknown:partialScope, not negative.
  23. Power over same-case history (histPower). The deciding court is the same court (any bench: withdrawal, substitution, rehearing), its successor, a higher court of the system, or SCOTUS. If the deciding court is unknown, the row is admitted as okUnverifiedBy.
  24. Federal circuits change the status only of decisions of their own circuit (v1).
  25. Certificates.
    • The target check is the presence of the citation (spacing and case ignored) or of every name token (≥ 3 characters) in the quote or window. Since the five-limits pass, a cite: evidence must also resolve through the citation index to the row's target when cite_index.tsv is supplied (item 64).
    • Window hashes are re-checked in Lean when window_sha.tsv is supplied (item 65).
    • Cue and disqualifier phrases are fixed lists in Certificate.lean.
  26. Holdings' certificates are checked for hash and quote-at-offset only. The role column stands in for the part.
  27. Findings.
    • appliesSupersededHolding in the citation pass uses the citing date as the conduct date (an upper bound on the real conduct date).
    • citesUnpublishedAsBinding needs an admitted followed treatment, since a bare citation does not say how it was used.
    • citesOverruled no longer needs the negating decision to bind the citing court: v1's condition was dropped in D4 triage, since status is not relative to the citing court (§5.1B, T1). See item 53.
  28. Splits.
    • Examined at the asOf date.
    • split rows follow DESIGN layer 5 (D4 triage): two holdings on the question with opposite answers, both good law on asOf, by courts (court, unit) neither of which binds the other (force known and below bindingAbsentConflict both ways), with no good-law holding of a non-trial court binding both. This test is in the runner glue; the Spec's resolver-based split and scotus_resolves_split now back only conflict rows.
    • conflict rows: the bound courts are every (court, unit) that holds on the issue, plus one trial court per system/circuit involved. Opposite permissible answers within one bound court are a conflict.
  29. Horty consistency is checked only where factors.tsv gives reasons. The checked base is the candidates with force binding after resolution.
Readings chosen in differential testing (DEVIATIONS.md 30–54)

Each item below is a place where the Lean and the Python reference differed and both now follow the reading given here. (c) marks a choice where doctrine.md leaves the answer open; (a) marks a Lean correction against doctrine, listed because it changes what the Lean computes. The reference records the same list in REF_NOTES.md (R-numbers in brackets).

  1. Supersession by enactment, issue - (a). A supersessions.tsv row with issue - reaches the target's admitted holdings whose issue cites the amended block: issues.usc equal to the law change's usc_block, or one a subsection of the other. With none, it reaches some issue, unknown which (someIssue). SEvent now carries a Scope (§7 AB1: issue-limited).
  2. retroactive_to = 1 (SCHEMA, 2026-11-12). The law governs cases pending on its effective date, whatever the conduct date. Pending-ness is not in the data, so this is approximated as: the supersession is known from the effective date (question date t >= effective) and reaches all conduct. A case decided after the effective date that was not pending on it is over-reached. [R30]
  3. Supersession evidence (a). A row whose evidence is laterCourtSays:<tid> is admitted only when that treatment row's text certificate passes. (c) A supersededByEnactment treatment alone changes no status: without the law change there is no effective date, retroactivity or amended block (AB1). [R27]
  4. Inferred rows (§9.26). An explicit = 0 treatment or supersession never changes status; it is atRisk only. [R26]
  5. Power with an unknown issue domain (a, D5). Power is decided per issue reached: a named holding on its own domain; ⊤, or an issue of unknown domain, on every domain it could have (each court's home domain, federal law, patent law when the Federal Circuit is involved). Disagreeing domains, or an unknown court epoch, admit the row unverified with the effect unknown powerUnknown (a new Unk reason; TEvent.powerKnown). A someIssue treatment is narrowed to the holdings the court has power over (Scope.someOf).
  6. Fallbacks for unknown attributes (c). An unknown publication is read as published, an unknown form as a full opinion, a missing trialScope row as statewide, a missing horizontal row as soft for force and strong for power, an unknown bench as a panel, a missing circulation row as not en banc, and an unknown (0) unit as not the own unit (for an appellate division over a trial court: no power). These are the Lean's existing assume* labels; the reference adopted them in place of enumerating the values. [R1, R31]
  7. Partial reach on ⊤ (c). Any event, negative or unknown, that reaches only part of a decision makes ⊤ unknown partialScope (§8.2 "partiallyNegative"). An unknown whole-decision event ranks above it. [R32]
  8. Revival (c). An overruling lapses while the overruling decision is withdrawn, substituted, vacated (also by an en banc grant that vacates under the court's rule), depublished, or reversed, each over the whole decision. It revives if that decision is reinstated (§5.1A). A partial event, review granted, an unknown en banc rule, or the overruler being overruled leaves the overruling standing: revival is not automatic (T3). [R15]
  9. Reinstatement (a). reinstated also ends a depublication and a pending review (§5.1A "restores status").
  10. Same-case power (a). A history row is decided by the target's own court, a successor, a higher court of its system that reviews it (federal: its own circuit, or the Federal Circuit), or SCOTUS. The Court of Federal Claims reviews no one. [R25]
  11. Trial courts (a, F13). A trial court or appellate division has no power over its own decisions.
  12. Adoption (a). An adopter may change the status of an adopted decision only from at least the decision's dated tier (Kentucky 1976), and then under its own horizontal rule (Bonner). An adopted decision belongs to no unit of the adopter.
  13. Federal Circuit (a, F11(b)). It has power over district courts on patent issues. From 1 Oct 1982 a regional circuit's patent law no longer binds its district courts.
  14. Plurality decisions (c, HD6). A majority or per curiam holding of a plurality decision binds. An equally divided decision caps at none, whatever role the reader gave the holding.
  15. Another state's law (c). A state court's ruling on a third system's law binds the system's own lower courts (vertical stare decisis), as on federal law.
  16. SCOTUS on state law (F1, "on federal questions only"): persuasive everywhere. The Lean already did this; the reference was corrected. [R10]
  17. Pre-Erie (c, DEVIATIONS 2). Federal decisions on state law before 25 Apr 1938 are persuasive in federal courts, the deciding circuit included. State high courts are persuasive in federal courts before Erie.
  18. E3 stateFollowsCircuit (a). Applies only to the court of appeals of the circuit the state lies in (28 U.S.C. § 41). The runner gives each state system its circuit from its courts' names (majority vote).
  19. Temporal scope unknown (c, TM2). Retroactive, for state law too: retroactivity is the general rule, and a prospective overruling must say so. [R14]
  20. California review granted (c, S-CA). Read only from the approved reviewGrantedForce rule. Data note: data/system_rules.tsv has no such row yet, so S-CA review grants have no effect on the real data. [R16]
  21. Court of last resort and the system horizontal row (c). A system-level row describes the intermediate courts; a court of last resort is bound by its own precedent only through a court-level row. Data note: the D.C. Court of Appeals' divisional rule (M.A.P. v. Ryan) needs a court-level row. [R23]
  22. Holdings (a). Admitted only through their own certificate (hash, quote at offset, role).
  23. History certificates (c). A quote from the target's own text needs no target evidence (Cert.Input.selfText). History kind other has no cue and cannot be certified. [R21, R28]
  24. Findings (a/c).
    • Citation findings are not made when every live effect behind the cited status is the citing decision's own.
    • Per-holding findings only when the citing decision holds on that issue, or holds on nothing and every holding of the cited decision is negative (HD4), and only when the whole decision is not already negative.
    • reversed is a citesVacated (§5.1A). [R29]
    • Treatment findings read only rows whose text certificate passed (and, in the reference, that are not earlier than their target).
    • panelDepartsWithoutEnBanc: status-changing kinds only, any bench short of en banc, only from good law.
    • pluralityTreatedAsBinding: a plurality decision with no Marks row that would bind the citing court as a majority opinion on every domain its issue could have.
    • citesUnpublishedAsBinding: below bindingAbsentConflict on every domain the issue could have, ignoring the cited decision's status (which has findings of its own).
    • atRisk inferredRejection: power not shown absent, and the target not already wholly negative.
    • firm (D2) is the same verdict with the S/L tables: the D5 class and the negative kind, not the unknown reason.
  25. Texas writ/pet. refused (a, S-TX-3). The notation promotes only a state intermediate court's opinion. On any other court it is a data error and changes nothing (it had demoted a circuit's binding force on its own district courts). [R24] Narrowed by item 62.
  26. Certificate target evidence (D4 real data). The target may be named in the quote or in any well-formed window covering it. Citations compare as lowercase letters and digits (SCHEMA's normalised cite:); names compare as whole words of at least 3 characters. Only well-formed windows (text length = end0 − start0) are used.
  27. Cues and disqualifiers. One cue table (Cert.cues, widened for "declines/refuse to follow", "reject", "certiorari granted"). Disqualifiers are phrases only (procedural rulings, reported history, refusals to overrule). A mention of a dissent is not a dissent's words; the part column decides that.
  28. Firm. Only U-tagged rows are infirm; untagged (-) v1 rows are data and firm.
  29. BAP (F13). A BAP changes no status. Same-case history: a BAP reviews its circuit's bankruptcy courts; in the federal system otherwise only a court of appeals reviews.
  30. Holdings windows are read from holdings_cert_text.tsv as well as cert_text.tsv.
  31. Open (c): a court whose tier changed (the D.C. Court of Appeals, intermediate to 1971, then last resort) acting on its own pre-change decisions. The Lean treats the later bench as a higher court; the reference treats it as the same court under its horizontal rule. 40 real residual rows; DIFFTEST.md §5.
The five limits (DEVIATIONS.md, second pass)
  1. Firm, by any route (c, DIFFTEST seed 30984). A citation finding is firm when the S/L-only tables make the same finding (the same kind on the same status) by any route: the whole decision, or holding by holding. Before, the whole-decision row's firm flag read only the whole-decision status. This is the reference's reading; the regression fixture is fixtures/regress/gen120-30984. atRisk citesLaterNegated had firm = 1 hard-coded; it is now computed.
  2. Texas writ and petition notations (a, S-TX-3, F3). A writRefused row promotes the target only when:
    • the target is a Texas intermediate decision (the system is found from court names, as for E3);
    • the wording is "writ ref'd"/"writ refused" dated before 1 Sept 1997, or "pet. ref'd"/"petition refused" from then on, and never "n.r.e.";
    • the case is civil: a known refusing decision must be the civil court of last resort's; when it is unknown, only a writ-era notation counts (the writ of error was civil only; a petition-era "pet. ref'd" may be a criminal PDR refusal). It is read from the certified quote in the runner (Run.writPromotes, HEvent.promotes). The 2,142 Louisiana "Writ refused." rows of snap4 no longer promote anything (the data agent has since relabelled them other). [REF L5]
  3. Commission opinions (H4, §3.2 TX). commission.tsv (optional) gives each decision its notation, and the adoption.tsv filters for the Texas Commission of Appeals are now read:
    • opinionAdopted takes "Opinion adopted", "Opinion approved" and "adopted as the opinion of the court"; holdingApproved and judgmentAdopted take their notations;
    • none takes a decision with no notation row, one whose wording the data could not classify (other), and every decision when commission.tsv is absent: an adoption that is not shown is no adoption (c);
    • resultOnly is read as persuasive (the force scale has no result-only grade, and every compared output cuts at bindingAbsentConflict);
    • a "Judgment adopted" notation on any court's decision (a commissioner opinion of the CCA or of Missouri) caps it at persuasive. The runner glue reads it as a memorandum form, because the locked scotus_binds_federal fixes the caps inside force;
    • an adopted decision ranks in the resolver as its adopter's (the Supreme Court of Texas: 3). Not modelled: power over an adopted commission opinion is still judged on the commission's own (special) tier.
  4. Citation index (SCHEMA addition: optional cite_index.tsv, normalised citation → node, derived from graph/cite_index.tsv restricted to the cited evidence by tools/caselaw2/cite_index_build.py). When it is supplied, a cite: evidence passes only if the citation occurs in the quote or a usable window and the index maps its compact form to the row's target (checkCert_cite_index). A compact key that two nodes share is left out: it is ambiguous and resolves to nothing (the real index has none). History rows whose quote is the target's own text still need no evidence. Name evidence keeps its rule.
  5. Window hashes (SCHEMA addition: optional window_sha.tsv with text_sha, start0, end0, sha1, src; written by tools/caselaw2/window_sha.py from the corpus text at git HEAD, after checking each file's SHA-1 against text_sha). When it is supplied, a window is usable only if its key has a recorded digest and the checker's own SHA-1 of the window text equals it; otherwise the row fails with windowHash (checkCert_window_hash). The SHA-1 is pure Lean (Sha1.hex, with #guard vectors from hashlib). Each window's digest is computed once per run, as a Thunk pinned to Sha1.hex text by Window.digest_eq.
  6. New finding kinds on both sides (c). Readings settled in D4:
    • ignoresBindingInUnit (§9 item 27): a trial-level state court with no power over the precedent declines to follow, or claims to overrule, a good-law precedent that binds it through its own unit (VownUnit, appDivBinds) on every domain the issue could have. The Lean's earlier, wider reading (also hWithinUnit and hStrong, which are panel departures) is dropped; those cases are panelDepartsWithoutEnBanc. A decision promoted by a writ or petition notation binds as the court of last resort's, not through the unit rule.
    • atRisk citesLaterNegated: the cited decision is wholly negative on asOf but not on the citing date, and a live negative effect comes from a decision whose court binds the citing court on that decision's date, on every domain. Supersessions, unknown deciding decisions and the citing decision itself do not count.
    • atRisk soft (limited, questioned, criticized, declinedToFollow) and atRisk claim (a status-changing kind by a court shown to lack power, T2): only for rows whose target is not later than the treating decision (T1), and not already wholly negative.
    • atRisk contraryBinding (F14): the earliest later contrary holding of a non-trial court that binds the holder's court on its date, on the issue's domain or on every domain an unknown one could have. The search stops when the holder is no longer good law.
  7. Conflict resolution (c, §1.2 F7, §4.1 V). For conflict rows the runner prepares the candidates before the Spec's resolve:
    • a candidate whose deciding court another candidate binds, without binding it back, is displaced; a decision held by binding adoption is displaced only by one that also binds its adopter;
    • first-in-time is the rule of the source court whose panels conflict, not of the bound court;
    • the trial-scope rule is the intermediate court's (a court-level trialScope row overrides the system row) and is already in the candidates' force, so resolve's own-unit step is not used;
    • a good-law holding whose force is unknown leaves the bound court undecided (no row, D5);
    • only holdings dated by asOf, and plurality holdings with a Marks row, count (the split filter); the firm run reads only S/L Marks rows;
    • answers are written as a set.
The hunt fixes and the WSL run (DEVIATIONS.md, last items; one is open)
  1. Divisions of a court of last resort (H6, §3.2/§4 DC; M.A.P. v. Ryan, 285 A.2d 310 (D.C. 1971)). A court of last resort with a court-level horizontal row (system = -court_id) is read as sitting in divisions. A division is bound by the court's own decisions as that row says (divisionRelation, forceDiv), and only an en banc–equivalent bench overrules them (lastResortBench). The court itself, en banc, is still not bound (relation's H1self), so nothing_binds_last_resort holds as locked: it speaks of the court, not of a division. Every force the runner computes is for the court as it ordinarily sits (forceDiv); forceDiv_eq_force proves this changes nothing for any court that is not a court of last resort. A system-level row does not make a court of last resort a divisional court. Decisions of the court's earlier, intermediate era fall to the higher-court rule (any bench), on both sides.
  2. Status after an adoption cut-off is per heir (H4, F10; Reach, reachOf, inLine, statusFor). Heirs are binding adoptions with filter all or unitB; persuasive adoptions and notation filters make none. A status-changing treatment reaches: every line if it is SCOTUS's; the original line if it is by the decision's own court, a court that replaced it (a succession other than a split), a higher court of its system, or an adopter once the original court has no epoch; an heir if the treating court is that heir, or stands above it, or the original line overruled on or before the heir's cut-off. A citing court is in an heir's line when it is the heir or a court below it (same system, lower tier; under a federal court of appeals, its circuit). Limits: (a) court epochs in courts2.tsv rarely end, so "the original court is gone" almost never fires: after a split that ended the old court (Alabama 1969), a successor's overruling reaches only its own line; (b) per-heir status is applied to the citation findings (cites*, citesLaterNegated, supersededConductUnknown) only. status.tsv, the treatment-level families, splits, conflicts and Horty bases still read the union status (negative if negative in any line).
  3. Superseded holdings need a conduct date and a holding-level match (H2, §7 AB1). SCHEMA carries no conduct date for a citing decision, and its own date is not one. appliesSupersededHolding therefore needs statusAtConduct = some … and is never emitted from the present data. The low-confidence family atRisk supersededConductUnknown:<issue> is emitted instead when (a) the cited holding is superseded for the latest conduct the citing decision could concern (its own date), and (b) the citing decision has a holding on the same issue, or on an issue whose US Code block is the block the superseding law rewrote. The old fallback (a citing decision with no holdings citing a decision all of whose holdings are negative) does not apply to it.
  4. Panel departures (H3b, F7). panelDepartsWithoutEnBanc needs a bench known to be a panel or a division (an unknown bench and an opinion circulated to the full court make no finding, whatever the circulation rule), and a strong or within-unit rule covering both the precedent's date and the treating date. A missing row makes no finding. A federal court of appeals makes none before 1 September 1948 (enBancStatuteDate, 28 U.S.C. § 46(c); tag L). Power is unchanged (a missing row still needs an en banc bench, R31), so status is unchanged. horizontal rows stay keyed by the precedent's date: dating a rule's start also ends the binding force of older decisions on the court's own panels, which is why the federal date is a constant and not a row date. Ohio (soft before 1 July 2010) and Louisiana (within-circuit from 1997) are dated in system_rules.tsv (tools/caselaw2/rule_dates_fix.py); those two dates are from memory (tag L) and need the courts agent's check.
  5. Texas notations that add no approval (a, sweep seed 51925). writPromotes now also excludes "denied", "dism.", "w.o.j." and the criminal "PDR" wordings, as the reference does.
  6. Closed (c): a split successor without a firm adoption row (round 2). Reading, on both sides: a split succession row never by itself makes the new court hold the old court's decisions. Only an adoption row does, and each run (all tables; S/L tables) reads its own adoption rows. rename, replace and absorb rows are unchanged. Grounds: a court made by dividing another does not take the old court's precedent by the division alone. The Eleventh Circuit took the former Fifth's by its own en banc decision (Bonner v. City of Prichard, 661 F.2d 1206, 1209 (11th Cir. 1981)); the Tenth Circuit, made from the Eighth in 1929, did not take the Eighth's (Estate of McMorris, 243 F.3d 1254, 1258 (10th Cir. 2001); doctrine F10). Alabama, Act No. 987 of 1969 (eff. 1 Oct 1969):
    • the Court of Appeals continued as the Court of Criminal Appeals (same court, same three judges): Coalite, Inc. v. Aldridge (Ala. Civ. App. 1969) says the case "was transferred from the Court of Appeals, now the Court of Criminal Appeals, to this, the Court of Civil Appeals, on October 1, 1969, pursuant to Act 987". A continued court holds its own decisions (H3). The court acts on that footing: "We overrule Willis, supra, so far as it might restrain us from acting ex mero motu" (Ala. Crim. App., 17 Aug 1971, node 110729, of a 1964 Court of Appeals decision). The adoption row 3 <- 1 is therefore verified and its tag moved U to S in data/adoption.tsv (round 2, one row; the original is adoption.pre_round2.tsv);
    • the Court of Civil Appeals was a new court. No decision or statute adopting the old court's decisions as its own was found in four searches. Its practice treats them as its precedent (it overruled Colquitt, a 1964 Court of Appeals decision, in 2007, node 106047), but that is practice, not an adoption shown. The row 2 <- 1 stays U, so findings that rest on it are firm = 0 on both sides. The Lean already read inheritance only from adoption rows. The reference's firm run let the successor hold the old court's decisions through the S-tagged succession row; it now reads a split as the Lean does. Expected on the 11 real firm flags: the 10 Court of Criminal Appeals keys become firm on both sides (data), the 1 Court of Civil Appeals key becomes not firm on both sides (reading).

Data gaps

Courts and decisions
  • bench
    • It is unknown for 3.19M decisions, mostly state courts of last resort, because there is no header cue. They are not assumed to be whole-court.
    • About 1 in 5 enBanc labels is still an order on a rehearing petition rather than a decision of the en banc court.
    • The en banc / circulated re-read (labels_fix2.py) covers only the 15,690 decisions that overrule, disapprove or recede. Even there about one in four en banc decisions is still panel: three-judge courts where the panel was the whole court, Alabama's appellate courts (always a full court), Louisiana five-judge benches, and decisions with no judges line. A court-size rule would be needed.
    • conflictPanel has only 5 samples (60%).
  • Units
    • Not recovered for about 38% of the decisions of unit-structured intermediate courts. The weakest are TX (45%), CA (55%), IN (56%) and NY AD (61%), mostly pre-1980 decisions with bare numeric dockets and no judge match.
    • NY Appellate Term, the OK Court of Civil Appeals and Tennessee are almost unrecovered.
    • Re-fetching CAP head_matter (which carries the court line) would close most of this gap; that was not attempted here.
    • County tables are the current ones:
      • Ohio: districts 11 and 12 are applied only from 1976.
      • Louisiana: applied from 1960.
      • Florida and Texas: no county tables are used, because their county-to-district maps changed or overlap.
  • Recall is not measured. The precision figures say nothing about recall. Header-only en banc and plurality detection misses en banc or plurality decisions whose header says nothing. Plurality is especially conservative: 199 decisions.
  • Publication
    • published relies on CAP's near-constant precedential_status. A reported state decision that a later court depublished is still "published": depublication is a same-case event and belongs in history.tsv.
    • Reporter check (labels_fix2.py): 8,022 reporter-cited decisions stay non-published because they say so themselves or are entries under 600 characters. A Florida per curiam of under 300 characters that cites an authority is still table.
    • The hunt's figure of 77,575 mislabelled decisions was too high: 50,512 are Florida PCAs without opinion and about 11,600 are T.C. Memo. / Summary Opinions, both correctly non-published. 7,342 were wrong and are fixed.
  • Form
    • SCOTUS memorandum orders (272,740) and short orders elsewhere (643,590) are form = memorandum. 371,105 stubs stay unknown: 48,586 at SCOTUS and 322,519 elsewhere (162,692 of those have no opinion text; the rest have no order language).
  • Doctrine tables
    • Rows marked U in doctrine.md stay U. The best readings are tagged U and are data, not premises.
    • Still uncertain: the California 1966 effective day; the Oklahoma 1959-03-11 date rests on a statutory history note (L); the end of the Delaware Court of Errors and Appeals in 1897 (day); TRAP 41.3's start (believed 2008-09-01, not confirmed; no row depends on it); the Ohio 2002 rule (secondary sources); the CNMI 2004 end of Ninth Circuit review (1 or 2 May).
  • Military courts stay tier S; CAAF binds the service Courts of Criminal Appeals through adoption.tsv.
  • Tribal courts are one system per tribe (1000–1022); their tiers are v1's (S), except Navajo (L), so a tribal appellate court does not yet bind its trial courts.
  • Unmapped: none. The 8 former 3160 decisions: 6 Department of the Interior land-office decisions → 10109 (federal, S); 1 Salina land-office register → 10110 (federal, S); Ex parte Rhodes (1816, "Judge's Chambers") → 10111, system 999 (state not identified; U).
  • Web checks (2026-11-12, limit 8): 19 of 25 searches; results above and in courts_validation.md §5. Earlier, 3 of the allowed 10 searches were used. They verified:
    • the Maryland 2022-12-14 renames;
    • Alabama Act No. 987, effective 1969-10-01;
    • D.C. Pub. L. 87-873, approved 1962-10-23 (effective date computed).
  • 2026-11-12 coordinator: added system_rules rows for CA reviewGrantedForce (system 5) and D.C. Court of Appeals court-level horizontal strong (court 627), the two data gaps DIFFTEST found.
Statutes
  • Citations are read only from 1995 on, so block-level links start in 1995; earlier decisions enter only through a reporter cite in a law or report (cite stratum, linked by section).
  • Block rewrites the record credits to an edition rather than a law (174,795 first rewrites in the overrides work) have no law, so no row here.
  • Law texts: govinfo PLAW starts with the 104th Congress; earlier laws (Civil Rights Act of 1991, etc.) have no text (record:...:notext), so no effective-date reading and no naming evidence.
  • Effective dates for rows the LLM did not read come from regex rules over the law's effective-date passages (src rx:<kind>:sec<n>:rank<r>; rank 0 = in the amending section, 1 = names it, 2 = its title, 3 = Act-wide), or the record's in-force day. See the regex accuracy line above.
  • quotedWordsStruck covers only the first rewrite of a cited block (decision-text features were not recomputed for later rewrites).
  • Committee reports: only those listed in the law's legislative-history note, part 1 of multi-part reports.
  • explicit for unaudited rows: the naming passage contains override language (overrul, supersed, in response to, reject the, restore, clarify that, ...); the audits show naming alone often means codification (see the codifies counts).
  • laterCourtSays and issue_key depend on the reader's treatments.tsv and the holdings agent's holdings.tsv/issues.tsv; rows are added by rerunning s7_write.py and s9_validate.py when those files exist.
Data and contract problems found in differential testing
  • d1. SCHEMA did not type the history and treatment id. The reader writes strings, and the Lean expected numbers (fixed on the Lean side as a1).
  • d2. data/system_rules.tsv has no reviewGrantedForce row, so California review grants have no effect on the real data. This is for the courts agent.
  • d3. There is no court-level horizontal row for the D.C. Court of Appeals, so M.A.P. v. Ryan's divisional rule is not applied. This is for the courts agent.
  • d4. stateFollowsCircuit rows name no circuit. The Lean now derives the circuit from court names, as the reference does.

What is tested, not proved, and what is assumed

  • Glue: the runner's TSV translation and output, Run.lean, Data.lean and Tsv.lean (about 860 lines). It is exercised by fixtures/ (all 13 SCHEMA files, every output kind) and a full-scale load and citation pass on synthetic decisions (6.89M nodes, 6.04M citations).
  • Glue fuzzing (FUZZ.md, tools/caselaw2/fuzz/):
    • Run A, 300 cases with Lean: the loaders reject and log every row SCHEMA rejects and parse every other row to the oracle's values; a re-serialised row loads back identically; Cert.quoteOk and its slice match Python's code-point slicing.
    • Run B: 5,000 cases against the reference only. Its Lean half awaits Application Control.
    • Every real certificate (346,835 rows) was recomputed in Python; there are 0 disagreements with the runner.
    • The open Lean bugs FB-L1 to FB-L8 are in FUZZ_BUGS.md.
  • The Horty check in the runner (factors.tsv) has not been exercised on fixtures.
  • Differential testing (D4) against the independent Python reference: done, see DIFFTEST.md. The final sweep of 5,000 fresh generated universes leaves a residual of under 0.01% of compared keys, all triaged. The real data run so far (supersessions on all 6.9M decisions) shows no disagreement.
  • The split rows are decided in the runner glue (DESIGN layer 5 pairwise test) and are tested only. The Spec's split/scotus_resolves_split back the conflict rows.
  • The doctrine tables: courts2, succession, adoption and system_rules, with their S/L/U tags.
    • Theorems never assume a row.
    • Verdicts carry firm = 1 when the S/L-only tables agree with the tables including U rows.
  • The readers: holdings text, issue keys, answers and Marks rows (held back by certificates for treatments and history; holdings only partly).
  • The departures listed in DEVIATIONS.md.
  • The Lean compiler, for compiled runs (runner/, lean_exe caselaw2) and #guard.
  • Windows Application Control blocks the locally built caselaw2.exe (since 12 Nov), so every run since then is interpreted: run_lean.sh falls back to lake env lean --run, and generated differential testing uses runner/RunBatch.lean (the built Run module, imported once per batch) through ref/drt.py. On 12 Nov at 19:32 the policy also began blocking the toolchain's lean.exe (unsigned), which stops every build and run until it is allowed again.

And the limit no proof removes: a passing certificate shows that these words, at this place, in this part of this court's opinion, warrant the row. It does not show the reading is legally right. That is measured by the audits and oracles in section 10, not proved.

13. Reproduce

Lean (from ~/Documents/global-law-lean/lean-proofs) and the runner (from ~/Documents/us-caselaw-lean-work/caselaw-lean-2):

lake build LegalProofs.CaseLaw2            # model + proofs + examples + mutation matrix + statement lock
python audit/audit.py check                # statement lock, axioms within {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}, no sorry
./run_lean.sh <shards> [data] [edges] [out] [asOf]   # the runner (compiled; falls back to the interpreter)
./run_lean_wsl.sh build | audit | run ...  # the same under Linux Lean in WSL (see "Running under WSL")

Differential testing (lean-proofs/tools/caselaw2/ref/) and the real-data diff:

python gen.py --seed S --rounds N [--n 60] --out DIR --ref --lean --diff
python regress.py
difftest/run_real.sh real3

Evaluation (lean-proofs/tools/caselaw2/eval/):

python score.py          # eval/results.json and eval/tables/*.tsv
python score.py --v1     # v1 on the same gold: eval/results_v1.json
python sampler.py <audit> <n>   # blind audit packets; seed 20261112

This report:

Items
1. Implicit-overruling tier (installed 23:24; DEVIATIONS 83)
  • Format. round3/implicit_schema.md, now in SCHEMA.md: a treatments row with a line in data/treatment_witness.tsv says "X was overruled by Y" in the words of a later decision W. Both checkers implement it: Lean Cert.checkWitness (Certificate.lean), wired in Run.lean; reference check_witness. Order of checks: witnessBadRow, the text checks on W's window, byUnresolved, targetLater, witnessEarlier, witnessNoStanding, then Y's power over X.
  • Effect. Never a status. One finding, atRisk X Y inferredRejection, while X is not already negative. No panel, unit or claim finding from a witness row.
  • Theorems (4, locked). Cert.witnessTail_sound, Cert.checkWitness_sound, Cert.checkWitness_inferred, and Examples.witness_row_no_effect: the event built from an admitted witness row has no status effect (a corollary of Spec.inferred_treatment_no_effect). Mutant M27 (a checker that takes a row marked explicit, or a court with no standing) is killed by the new property. 12 new #guards.
  • Rows. 185 of the 189 round-3 candidates (the 4 that fail the work-folder verifier left out), plus 14 of the 21 round-2 rows converted from "by = the stating court" to "by = Y" (13 where W cites Y in the window, and Roberts by name). 199 staged.
  • Blind audit, 24 rows, two readers (the four landmark rows and 20 at random; passage and claim only). The court states it: 24/24. X right: 24/24. Y right: 21/24 (Wilson 95%: 69%–96%). The two witness rows with an unclear Y were removed before install. The third is the Lochner row, an old-format row whose by-decision is the stating court; it is kept and described as such.
  • Installed: 197 treatment rows added and 14 removed (the converted originals); treatment_witness.tsv 179 rows; cert_text +174, window_sha +174, cite_index +288. In the final run 167 of the 204 implicit rows are ok; 9 fail witnessNoStanding; the rest fail power or date order and assert nothing.
  • Files: work/round4/implicit_stage.py, work/round4/implicit/ (staged deltas, audit sheets, key, answers).
2. One cue table (DEVIATIONS 85)
  • tools/caselaw2/cues/cue_table.json is the only table. gen_cues.py writes LegalProofs/CaseLaw2/CueTable.lean, ref/cue_table.py and reader/cue_table.py; gen_cues.py --check fails on a stale copy. Cert.cues, Cert.disqualifiers, the reference's VERBS/DISQUALIFY_*, rules2.CUES2/DISQUAL2 and the implicit generator's table all read it.
  • The difference was two cues the reader had and the checkers lacked: "abrogat" for supersededByEnactment, "no longer" for questioned. The shared table has both. noCue on treatments: 41 → 0 (the 29 of round 3 and 12 older rows). Neither kind changes a status.
3. Sweep residue (DEVIATIONS 82 and 86; round4/sweep.md)
  • The three universes of round 3 (62003, 62350, 62391; 10 keys): Lean was wrong. candFor ranked a Texas decision promoted by "writ refused" at its own tier, although forceOn already treated it as the Supreme Court of Texas's. Fixed in Exec/Verdicts.lean. Round 3's note that the court had no earlier epoch was incorrect.
  • The final sweep then found the mirror case (63322, 3 keys): the reference was wrong (no precedence step between a writ-refused decision and an unpromoted one of the same court). Fixed in _resolve.
  • All four universes are in fixtures/regress/r4-*. Final sweep: 0 of 500.
6. Reader queue: the 11 answered packs (round4/queue.md)
  • Certified and installed: 161 treatment rows (treatments 35,021 → 35,182 before the implicit install). ans_142.jsonl (partial) was set aside as ans_142.partial.
  • Blind read of 20 new rows by the fork itself (it could not spawn readers): own act 18/20 (70%–97%), target 20/20, kind 13/20. The two rows shown wrong were removed. t:6865583:6852906:48056, which round 3 left installed, was removed again.
  • install.py re-adds rows removed after an audit on every run. Not fixed: the three ids must be removed again after any later run.
  • 246 packs (about 19,600 items) remain unread.
7. The rise of panelDepartsWithoutEnBanc (DEVIATIONS 84; round4/panel.md)
  • The 334 findings added in round 3 all come from the queue rows. Blind read of 20 (by the fork itself): the finding is sound in 1 (Wilson 1%–24%). In 18 the panel says circuit precedent "is no longer good law" after an intervening Supreme Court or state high court decision: the recognised exception to the prior-panel rule. Overruled-versus-disapproved confusion, bench labels and court labels were each 0 of 20. The status rows are right.
  • Fix, both engines: the finding needs the panel's own overruling words in the certified quote (overrul, disapprov, recede(s/d/ing) from). 998 → 573 (the count on the round-3 data was 571; 2 come from new rows). It removes 318 of the 334 new findings and 109 older ones.
  • The rise of atRisk (65,533 → 85,827 in round 3) was not audited. It is mostly citesLaterNegated (62,792 rows), which follows mechanically from every new status row.

2. Per-heir status everywhere
  • Before: per-heir status applied to the citation findings only (DEVIATIONS 69).
  • After: a new module Spec/Lines.lean and DEVIATIONS 74–79. Per-heir rows are written to a new file out/status_lines.tsv (the status.tsv columns plus line: orig or the heir's court id), only where a line-limited effect exists. status.tsv keeps the union status and its old format, because several tools read it by position. Splits and conflicts are judged with each holding's status in the line of the court asked about. Horty binding bases hold a precedent only if it is good law in that court's line (out/horty.tsv).
  • Theorems: 114 → 137, all 23 new ones locked. Among them lineStatus_heir_agrees, heldIn_ignores_unreaching, conflict_in_line_ignores_unreaching, mem_lineBase_iff, and the reductions to the union definitions when no heir exists (lineStatus_all, heldIn_all, lineBase_all, statusFor_le_status).
  • Mutants: M23–M26 added; the matrix is 26 × 26 and complete. 35 new #guards (Bonner, Salinas–Adamson, M.A.P., CCPA).
  • Reference: implemented by a separate subagent from the written reading only. It now also computes Horty binding bases, so Horty is compared for the first time. diff.py compares two more files (lines, horty). The generator has a new lines layer.
  • Real data: 622 per-line rows; 301 keys compared, 0 disagreements. 44 Horty bases compared, 0 disagreements.

Next round. One open sweep class: conflict rows that only the reference reports, at an adopter of a ceased court or a trial court below it (17 of 4,977 conflict keys in 500 universes; generator layer only, none on real data). Three readings the reference chose where DEVIATIONS 74–78 are silent agree with the Lean on every compared key but are not yet written into DEVIATIONS. The self bases and the Horty finding rows are still Lean only.
